title: 11th Edition Detachment Focus: Aquilan Shield
content:
Following hot on the heels of the Emperor’s Angels come his Praetorian Guard. The Adeptus Custodes get an early 11th edition Codex, and with it a slew of new rules and Detachments. In this article, we’re taking a look at the Aquilan Shield Detachment.

The Aquilan Shield are staunch defenders of the Imperium's most important servants, holding the line until they have fulfilled whatever key duty is their destiny. Their Shield Host Detachment provides durability and withering firepower to achieve this end.

Thanks to Games Workshop for providing us with a review copy of this codex and a provisional version of the Munitorum Field Manual. Any rules or points costs we reference are subject to change until they are published on the Warhammer 40K App.

Aquilan Shield

Detachment Cost: 1 DP

Force Disposition: Take and Hold

Unique: SHIELD HOST

If you dream of golden hosts mowing down ranks of the unworthy with ranged superiority, Aquilan Host indulges that fantasy more than any other Shield Host. This is the ‘shooty’ Detachment for your core Custodes, rewarding you for sitting on objectives and pouring bullets from the windows, as to deny any intruders entry. Moreover, this is also the Detachment that best-utilizes Aquilon Terminators, so if you’re excited to deploy a number of those gorgeous new plastic sculpts, this is the premier option to get them on the table.

Shield Captain - Credit: keewa

Detachment Rule: Gilded Guardians

While on an objective, enemy ranged attacks have -1 to wound your non-MONSTER/VEHICLE ADEPTUS CUSTODES whose toughness is less than the enemy’s strength. I feel like this could have been keyworded by now, given the frequency with which it appears. Regardless of how common this is, it’s still a welcome ability to have, given how resilient Custodes are in the new book.

Your standard Custodian statline is T7, with Terminators being T8, and given S14 isn’t exactly common, oftentimes Gilded Guardians reads as ‘your opponent wounds Custodes on objectives on 4+ at best’. For those around for the old Transhuman Physiology, that should strike fear in your heart. This Detachment ability really makes the +1T that your infantry received in this book soar, as while Lascannons and other S12 is common, were they T6, very little wounds modern Custodes on 2s.

Favored Ka’tah: Salvus

When selecting Salvus as your Ka’tah, shooting attacks gain 6” of range. This isn’t a massive deal for most Custodes units that have access to Ka’tahs, as your average guardian spears and axes have ranges of ~18”-24”. Where this comes up is with the units that benefit most from Aquilan Shield as a Detachment, which we’ll soon talk more about: Aquilon Terminators. Both the Adrathic Combi-destructor & Infernus Firepike have a range of merely 12”, so an extra 6” matters immensely in terms of getting that damage where it needs to be. This can also make attaining the extra shots from [RAPID FIRE] weapons a bit easier, and go figure, Aquilons also have that option via Lastrum Storm Bolters.

Enhancements

  • Pareldor’s Cruciatrix (30pts): ADEPTUS CUSTODES model only. Once per battle, at the start of any phase, the bearer heals D3+3 wounds. The premium paid for wounds of Custodes means that even if this is 4 more, it’s still likely worth it...so long as you guarantee the model survives to heal. That’s not difficult, but if the bearer gets cleared in a single phase, you’re down both the model and the speculative 4-6 wounds from the Cruciatrix. Whether the model is leading a unit or not is another consideration, as this heal doesn’t spill over (being just a heal on the enhanced model), so if your opponent undershoots and only deals ~2 damage to the bearer while clearing their squad, is it worth popping? This is a powerful tool, but requires some pregame math into key matchups to not waste. As a final note, annoyingly this doesn’t work with the Gilded Champion stratagem from Auric Champions, as it’s (Once per battle, per army) rather than (Once per battle, per unit), which would otherwise be a great plug-and-play synergy.
  • Not a Shell Wasted (10pts): ADEPTUS CUSTODES INFANTRY model only. The bearer’s unit’s ranged attacks have +1A. In any of your 3-model squads with a leader, this is usually +4A, so you’d prefer to use this on a squad where the relative volume increase has more impact than just extra shots on a profile that’s already [RAPID FIRE]-ing. Surprise surprise, it’s Aquilon Terminators once more, with a 50% increase in shots for their Combi-destructors.

Stratagems

  • Manoeuvre and Fire (1CP): During your Movement phase, when your ADEPTUS CUSTODES unit makes a fall back move, target it to also be able to shoot and charge that turn. This is a great tool to have, given your units are more likely to survive a combat than basically anything else in the game. On units which actively want to both shoot and fight in melee, this does double duty, but frankly most Custodes profiles do both admirably as a baseline, so it’s rare not to get max value from this stratagem.
  • Tip of the Talon (1CP): During your Shooting phase, when your ADEPTUS CUSTODES unit is selected to shoot, target it to gain +1S for that attack against enemy units within 9”. The only time you’ll use this stratagem is when it results in hitting a relevant breakpoint, and therefore this is effectively just +1 to wound in shooting...with a sizable asterisk. On weird profiles like Combi-destructors, which are -2/3D in spite of a measly S5, suddenly getting to wound the new Terminator statline on 4s helps put the hurt on TEQs. Similarly, this pushes many of your Vehicles’ best shooting to wound hulls on 3s, so cracking Land Raiders/Land Fortresses is far easier. This won’t come up in every matchup, but given that Aquilan Shield is the dedicated shooting Detachment for Custodes, it’s great to turn 5s to 4s, and 4s to 3s on relevant targets.
  • Rapid Reactions (1CP): During your opponent’s Movement phase, when an enemy unit falls back from your ADEPTUS CUSTODES INFANTRY unit, you can target it to make normal shooting attacks against only that enemy unit that fell back. This is one of the most punishing stratagems we’ve seen in recent memory, and is likely one you’ll retain a spare CP for, even just as a deterrent. While there’s a volume problem with a lot of Custodes shooting, especially with the overall reduction in unit sizes throughout the book, the fact you still get to hit on 2s for the vast majority of profiles means those paltry shots *will* convert, and *will* clear MEQs. The units you’re taking in this Detachment ought to excel at both shooting & melee, and the guns on most of your infantry are nothing to scoff at.

Detachment Combos

In spite of explicitly calling out that its Detachment rule doesn’t work with monsters or vehicles, this is likely the best Shield Host to pair with Grav-assault Force, for the fact that your tank profiles dearly appreciate fall back & shoot and the extra +1S from Aquilan’s stratagem toolbelt. With your tanks losing access to Ka’tahs (no more tank karate, sorry folks), it’s a bit of an uphill battle to make them worth building around. If you’re looking for trade pieces though, the Pallas being able to Deep Strike and push its guns to S11 isn’t anything to shrug at, especially given you can then scoot it backwards from the required <9”, and push in with Custodes (who in turn threaten Rapid Reactions). Furthermore, given the cost of everything, you tend to be more keen to burn a CP rather than points to access the ability to pull something like a Caladius from melee and fire into a key threat.

Given the benefits to Aquilon Terminators as well, it makes sense to consider Lions of the Emperor in order to better reposition your squads and have access to Fury of the Emperor. After all, Rapid Reactions isn’t worth much if you can’t actually get in, and tempt your opponent to fall back.

Is It Good?

Credit: Corrode

Unlike the other books of 11th edition so far, the design of Codex: Adeptus Custodes has severe locks placed on Shield Hosts, so where you might say Aquilan Shield is good in another book, it has to be *better* than other options here to see significant play. That’s not as clear, unfortunately. A lot of the tools here are designed explicitly for use with a unit that’s solid, but not extraordinary (in reference to Aquilon Terminators), and elsewhere the benefits of super-Salvus can fall flat. Custodes can Deep Strike or move quick enough that an extra 6” of range isn’t amazing, and playing the faction as a ‘stand and shoot’ army without access to Hidden retention leaves you vulnerable to get traded-up against by a shootier foe. If you find yourself playing against melee armies or those with a ton of 3W 2+/4++ profiles, Aquilan Shield seems amazing, but its cracks show compared to other Shield Hosts when facing superior ranged firepower.

Final Thoughts

For as much as this Detachment seeks to buff Custodes shooting, the steps taken to allow most available profiles to wound things tougher than a Terminator on better than a 5+ are slim. Certainly this can be offset by, as stated, taking a few Vehicles and using your on-foot Custodes to deal with things of Toughness 6 or less, but against skew lists like Knights I expect frustration from pilots of Aquilan Shield.

If you get out-shot, or are paired into an army that’s better at standing on objectives than you (again, Knights) a lot of the luster of this Detachment fades. You absolutely need to supplement your core of Terminators with proper S10/12 firepower, and recognize matchups where protecting something like a Pallas or two is the difference between victory and defeat. This Detachment can excel, but it requires a meta with minimal vehicle-heavy skew, and a player willing to understand difficult matchups; it’s not as easy to pilot as it first appears, especially in the face of other Custodes options. If tanks still knew karate, we’d be singing a different tune here at Tabletop Battles.

title: 11th Edition Detachment Focus: Honoured Companions
content:
Following hot on the heels of the Emperor’s Angels come his Praetorian Guard. The Adeptus Custodes get an early 11th edition Codex, and with it a slew of new rules and Detachments. In this article, we’re taking a look at the Honoured Companions Detachment.

If you want to field a stalwart army of classic Custodians, the Honoured Companions have you covered, providing reliable power for these dauntless defenders. This powerful Detachment spices up your battleline forces, making them even more potent than their upgraded statlines already do!

Thanks to Games Workshop for providing us with a review copy of this codex and a provisional version of the Munitorum Field Manual. Any rules or points costs we reference are subject to change until they are published on the Warhammer 40K App.

Honoured Companions

Detachment Cost: 1 DP

Force Disposition: Take and Hold

Honoured Companions is a 1DP Detachment that provides benefits for what we might call the “normal” Custodes. These are the ones on foot who walk around slaughtering people for the Emperor with spears, swords and occasionally axes. The Detachment makes their weapons hurt a bit more and gives them multiple ways of moving around the battlefield, without regard to trivial issues like whose turn it is or being locked in melee. These are also some of the cheapest units available to Custodes players, making this the closest thing to the “horde” army. You’ll almost certainly field numbers of models reaching into double figures. Custodian Sentinels. Credit: Pendulin

Detachment Rule: Companion’s Watch

Trusted Sentinel units get to reroll 1s to wound when in range of an objective. Trusted Sentinel is a keyword that applies to Custodian Guard, Sentinel Guard and Wardens. It’s a simple and effective buff, working on their ranged attacks as well as melee. It combines well with other abilities in the codex which provide rerolls to hit instead.

Enhancements

  • Arae Shrike (20pts): Enemy units can’t make Ingress Moves within 12” of this Adeptus Custodes Infantry model’s unit. People who want to fire meltas at you will have to walk. This is incredibly good, especially because it measures to the whole unit, not just the bearer, so planting a squad of Wardens or Sentinel Guard on the central objective becomes a nightmare for some armies to deal with.
  • Celeritous Sentinels (15pts, Upgrade): Your unit of Trusted Sentinels can do Heroic Interventions for 1 fewer CP and this doesn’t stop you doing more Heroic Interventions. In theory you could have three units charge in the enemy turn for free, or four if you’re prepared to pay a CP.

Stratagems

  • Emperor’s Domain (1CP): When Trusted Companions consolidate, they can always choose Objective Consolidation, regardless of the normal restrictions. This means your unit can leave melee so long as it ends up on an objective. They probably won’t have to go far as the Detachment rule incentivises your dudes to hang out on objectives. The enemy might just consolidate right back into melee with you if it’s your turn of course, so this is more for either reacting in the enemy turn and/or escaping units that are already tied up with your other stuff.
  • Avenge the Fallen (1CP): In the Fight Phase, a unit that’s below starting strength gets +2A on all its weapons, though not those of any attached Characters. Your opponent will learn to take units of one or two Custodes very seriously. This is especially nasty if a unit of 3 Wardens with axes loses a model, giving them 1 more attack than at full strength.
  • Swift as the Eagle (1CP): If an enemy unit moves within 8” of a Trusted Sentinel unit in their movement phase, you can do a normal move of D3+3”. Reactive moves like this are always great and the fact you can count on a minimum of 4” with this makes it even better. You might be able to combine this with a Shield Captain’s Surge move and/or Heroic Intervention.

Detachment Combos

This is tricky because you probably take one of the Shield Hosts, all of which are great. If you’re taking a lot of Sentinel Guard then you might not want to go for Aquilan Shield or Shadowkeepers, as their abilities duplicate what Sentinels do already. Personally I like Solar Watch, as the extra 2” of movement from the Calistus Ka’Tah will help your infantry get across the board, leaving nowhere for the Emperor’s perfidious enemies to hide.

Then it’s pretty much any of the other unit-specific options. Auric Champions if you plan to have a lot of characters leading your units or Might of the Moritoi to provide some even more mighty back up for your infantry would probably be my top picks. 

Lions of the Emperor for a few uppy-downy Terminators would be handy, to double down on the infantry “horde” approach without losing board coverage. However, you get so few units in a Custodes army that splitting your buffs between two armour types often isn't the way to go. Grav-assault Force offers the scary possibility of having several Coronus, each with two or three small units inside, using the Combat Deployment upgrade and 10” moves from Solar Watch to explode all over an enemy army. 

You might not need a Null Maiden Vigil all that much, since you’ll be focusing on the Custodes Battleline units for objectives, but it definitely wouldn’t be useless. Battle-shocking the enemy is a great way to claim objectives, after all.

Is It Good?

Adeptus Custodes Wardens by Crab-stuffed Mushrooms

Yes. Having your Custodes move around in and out of LoS or melee pretty much at will is extremely good, especially in the hands of a good player. This Detachment interacts really well with objectives, which is good news if you want to win games. It’s definitely better against enemies who want to come towards you to fight in melee. They’ll have a really tricky time fighting your excellent units while they dodge and weave about the place. Shooting armies won’t have as much difficulty from the Detachment, though they’ll still have the very real problem of being chopped into little bits.

Final Thoughts

Detachments that improve Battleline units are always interesting because they tend to affect lots of your army. Honoured Companions is a bit unusual as these kinds of Detachments tend to provide fairly simple buffs, whereas this instead gives all kinds of movement-based tricks. For mere mortals it’ll take a bit of practice to make the most of all the movement shenanigans possible for Honoured Companions but a good player will run shiny golden rings around people.

title: 11th Edition Detachment Focus: Solar Watch
content:
Following hot on the heels of the Emperor’s Angels come his Praetorian Guard. The Adeptus Custodes get an early 11th edition Codex, and with it a slew of new rules and Detachments. In this article, we’re taking a look at the Solar Watch Detachment.

Swift death awaits any who dare to breach the sanctity of Terra, with the Solar Watch standing vigilant ready to intercept any threat to the throneworld. What does that look like in-game? Let's find out.

Thanks to Games Workshop for providing us with a review copy of this Codex and a provisional version of the Munitorum Field Manual. Any rules or points costs we reference are subject to change until they are published on the Warhammer 40K App.

Solar Watch

Detachment Cost: 1 DP

Force Disposition: Reconnaissance

Unique: SHIELD HOST

So you wanna go fast but hate thinking about playing models that might actually die like the Aeldari? There is no better way to bring your fight to (or perhaps run away from) your foes than by running the Shield Host with the job of protecting the Sol System. The Solar Watch is a 1 DP Shield Host Detachment that focuses on maintaining and manipulating movement on the battlefield. As the key to clinching so many battles often comes down to being in the right place at the right time, the Solar Watch is a great way to establish board control.

Custodes Vertus Praetors. Credit: Jack Hunter

Detachment Rule: Talon Sortie

Adeptus Custodes units that elect to make a fall-back move are still eligible to charge. With the big bumps to speed and endurance that Custodes have seen across the board, any ability that keeps them from being bogged down in the wrong fights or that lets them make the most of their limited activations is a good one to have. Given that every model in the Custodes army is a stone cold killer this ability can make solving the meat mountain problem a really difficult one for your opponents

Favoured Ka’tah: Calistus

Each time a unit activates the Calistus Ka’tah they gain +2" to their movement characteristic. Calistus is one of the least flashy Ka’tahs in the Custodes arsenal but in lists built around the Solar Watch it is easily the most powerful and you will frequently find yourself activating it for at least half the units in your army round to round as it lets you move through all types of models when making normal/fall-back/charge moves while also pushing your standard foot custodes to a blistering 10" of speed.

With access to so many ways to get advance and charge or assault on your units from the myriad other Detachments, you quickly end up with an army of T7 jetbikes without the need for the bike itself (though there’s no reason not to slot a few into your list anyway since we’re going full Talladega Nights over here). 

Enhancements

  • Sally Forth (30pts): This enhancement is for Shield-Captains only and allows them to select a friendly Adeptus Custodes Infantry unit within 6" at the start of your Charge Phase and give them advance and charge. Just a straight up powerful enhancement to have at your fingertips, which a lot of factions would love to have in their back pocket.

    Wings: You're pretty much always taking this if you're playing this Detachment (unless you're going all bikes), it's one of the big draws.

  • Auric Eagle (15pts, Upgrade): This unit upgrade gives a single Adeptus Custodes Infantry or Mounted unit (but not terminators, they’re not allowed to have fun) +1 to their advance and charge rolls. Nothing to see here really but if you have the 15 to spend, as you sometimes will with Custodes there’s nothing wrong with going even faster. This also works well with a Blade Champion thanks to their built-in re-rolls to these.

Stratagems

  • Inexorable (1CP): During your movement phase, when an Adeptus Custodes unit is selected to move it may ignore modifiers to your unit’s movement, advance and charge rolls. Just a solid situationally useful Stratagem though keep in mind it also shuts down your modifier from Calistus.
  • At Spear’s Length (1CP): When an Adeptus Custodes unit is selected to make a fall-back move it can still shoot. Great for getting absolutely every bit of power out of your units as they careen around the board like my kids at the trampoline park, but with ancient archaeotech weaponry at their disposal instead of just ADHD and a lack of impulse control.
  • Gravimetric Grenade (1CP): Oh how an old favorite has fallen…At the start of your opponent’s charge phase an unengaged Adeptus Custodes unit may target a visible enemy unit within 12" and reduce any attempted charge rolls it makes by 1. This isn’t the old Allarus grenade of old that would send Death Guard players into apoplectic fits when their movement was reduced to -2 but it still has its place as a deterrent in the off chance your opponent actually wants to engage you.

Detachment Combos

Solar Watch goes well with just about any combination of Detachments in the book. It is easy to lean on Jet Bikes in a Detachment with this much speed but with how much Custodes want to be able to freely move about the board there really aren’t any bad choices for it. I’m personally a big fan of combining this with Might of the Moritoi for even more devastating dreadnoughts that absolutely will never be locked down but there are pretty strong arguments for anything outside of the Grav Assault Force. Venetari Lances are particularly brutal here as you can set up some really deep assassination runs by jacking their movement up to 14, hitting them with Auric Eagle and then launching them halfway across the board with ease to land their Precision strikes.

Is It Good?

Allarus Custodes from the Solar Watch Shield Host painted by Crab-stuffed Mushrooms

While I’d argue that the stratagems available to the Solar Watch aren’t the flashiest (though Fall-back and shoot is always welcome), the rest of the package is great for anyone looking to make the most out of their limited model count these days and those stratagems can easily be sublimated by the fact that this baby is only 1 DP.

Final Thoughts

If you ain’t first you’re last and I see no better way to take up as much space as possible if even the dice fail you than by running the Solar Watch. And yes, White is a pain in the ass to paint, but Custodes models take to it really well.

title: 11th Edition Detachment Focus: Shadowkeepers
content:
Following hot on the heels of the Emperor’s Angels come his Praetorian Guard. The Adeptus Custodes get an early 11th edition Codex, and with it a slew of new rules and Detachments. In this article, we’re taking a look at the Shadowkeepers Detachment.

Even amongst the Adeptus Custodes, some duties are uniquely grim, and for those dark tasks the Shadowkeepers are unleashed. Let's find out what that looks like on the tabletop.

Thanks to Games Workshop for providing us with a review copy of this Codex and a provisional version of the Munitorum Field Manual. Any rules or points costs we reference are subject to change until they are published on the Warhammer 40K App.

Shadowkeepers

Detachment Cost: 1 DP

Force Disposition: Purge the Foe

Unique: SHIELD HOST

The Shadowkeepers are the Shield Host devoted to tracking down and imprisoning all the scariest things the Imperium doesn’t want you to know about. They’re tasked with being the SCP unit in a universe where we think the horrors are already out and about and this Detachment emphasizes this with a suite of abilities and strats that are aligned with holding objectives, fear, and pinning things down.

Shadowkeeper Allarus Custodes. Credit: Pendulin

Detachment Rule: Wardens of Darkness

Melee attacks that target friendly non-vehicle/monster Adeptus Custodes units within the range of an objective with Strength greater than their Toughness have -1 to wound rolls. Custodes units are already hard to move and adding -1 to wound without having to field Sentinel Sodalities is a sweet treat when playing the objective game while giving a ‘defend the prison’ vibe.

Favoured Ka’tah: Kaptaris

When readying the Kaptaris Ka’tah, Shadowkeepers units can select one enemy unit engaged with them and force them to make a battle shock roll at -1. The same unit cannot be selected more than once for this ability (boooo). As we’ve begun to learn in the early days of 11th edition, battle-shock is a far more powerful effect than it has ever been. This is a nice-to-have effect for sure when you need it, though perhaps less effective than in other armies where you’re not often planning on just straight killing what is touching you.

Enhancements

  • Genalchemic Warding (30pts): Usable on any Adeptus Custodes model, this grants them a 5+ Feel No Pain. Pricey but so are your characters and keeping them alive seems good. 
  • Unstoppable Destroyer (25pts): Adeptus Custodes Infantry model only, this upgrade allows the unit to move up to 4 inches for their pile-in/consolidation moves and, more importantly, they can choose any consolidation mode when making a consolidation move regardless of the before moving restrictions. This is an insanely powerful ability for sneaking onto objectives or slipping into/out of combats you find yourself staring into the face of and is reason enough to take this Detachment on its own. While most things a Custodes’ player touches in close combat will evaporate, in the times where it doesn’t this will win you the game. Always remember that they’re not stuck in with you, you’re stuck in with them. 

Stratagems

  • Grim Responsibility (1CP): During the Fight phase when an Adeptus Custodes Infantry unit is selected to fight, that unit’s melee attacks gain Lethal Hits: Character/Monster. Decent stratagem to have when surrounded by giant bugs and daemons given the weight of attacks an Adeptus Custodes unit can put out.
  • No Escape (2CP): During your opponent’s Movement phase when an enemy unit completes a Fall-Back move, one friendly unengaged Adeptus Custodes unit that is within 6 inches of said unit that has fallen back may declare a charge. When selecting charge targets you can only select enemy units that have made a fall-back move this phase and are within maximum charge distance. Now THIS is a spicy meatball and well worth the 2CP. Being able to force ongoing combats and halt cheeky fallback maneuvers is huge. Also, note the timing on this one as there are situations where you’ll be able to wait out all of your opponent’s fallbacks if you find yourself in a real cluster and then pick the juiciest target when everything is said and done, though you do open your opponent up to being able to sidestep your best targets if you wait too long.
  • Indomitable Guardians (1CP): During your Fight Phase, when an enemy unit has fought, you can select an Adeptus Custodes unit that is within range of an objective and that is eligible to fight with this stratagem. That unit gains the Fights First special rule and must be the next unit selected to fight. We’ve seen this stratagem for Custodes before and it has always been great as 1 CP interrupts are hard to find.

Detachment Combos

As with most of the Custodes Shield Host Detachments their power is pretty-self contained. If you believe that battle-shocking is your favorite way to play this is a great Detachment to team up with the Null-Maiden Vigil. Otherwise I kind of like Honoured Companions here. Honoured gives you a second reactive move in your arsenal and the potential to have two units ignoring consolidation rules to really mess with your opponent’s control of the board AND furthers your gameplan of being extra good at standing on objectives with Companion’s Watch. 

Is It Good?

Custodian Sentinels. Credit: Pendulin

Shadowkeepers has some great stratagem support and one helluva enhancement but suffers from the fact that there are Shield Hosts that are just objectively better from a straightforward power perspective. Still, it isn’t necessarily a bad choice as it opens up some interesting play patterns and allows for some incredible objective play.

Final Thoughts

Aesthetically, Shadowkeepers is my favorite looking Custodes army with its dark colors and gold trim and I do see some really fun play lines for an army that wants to lean more into the Custodian Guard and less into the other toys Custodes can bring to the table. It’s just neat.

title: 11th Edition Detachment Focus: Lions of the Emperor
content:
Following hot on the heels of the Emperor’s Angels come his Praetorian Guard. The Adeptus Custodes get an early 11th edition Codex, and with it a slew of new rules and Detachments. In this article, we’re taking a look at the Lions of the Emperor Detachment.

Terminators! They're really good in the Custodes book! Lions of the Emperor! It's also really good. Updated to a 1DP option in the new Codex, Lions is now fully dedicated to supporting Terminators, and it does that really well, potentially being one of the most powerful choices in the Codex.

Thanks to Games Workshop for providing us with a review copy of this Codex and a provisional version of the Munitorum Field Manual. Any rules or points costs we reference are subject to change until they are published on the Warhammer 40K App.

Changelog

  • 2026-10-03 (Current): Updated for 11th Edition Codex
  • 2025-03-11: Original Publication

Lions of the Emperor

Detachment Cost: 1 DP

Force Disposition: Disruption

The Terminator armor-clad members of the Adeptus Custodes have mastered repeated use of teleportarium technology to always be in the right place at the right time and this Detachment emphasizes this with enhancements and stratagems tailored solely for the Allarus and Aquillan units in your army.

Allarus Custodes by Crab-stuffed Mushrooms

Detachment Rule: On Gilded Wings

At the end of your opponent’s fight phase if a friendly Adeptus Custodes Terminator unit is unengaged, you can place them in strategic reserves. Long time Adeptus Custodes players will recognize this as the old From Golden Light rule that Allarus and Aquilon have had for some time, however the once per battle rider has been removed. With the big point hikes to Custodes units that came with this Codex, having the ability to freely hop around the field turn after turn is obviously useful.

Enhancements

  • Leonine Ferocity (20pts): A single Shield-Captain in Allarus Terminator Armour may take this enhancement. Once per phase per army this unit can be targeted with the Rapid Ingress stratagem regardless of if the strat has already been used and at -1 CP. This use of Rapid Ingress also does not prevent the use of further Rapid Ingresses this phase. If you’re going all in on the Gilded Wings ability you’re often going to find yourself wanting to pop Rapid Ingress turn-after-turn to get the most out of your uppy-downy girls and boys which makes this enhancement a contender when you have 20 points lying around and you actually chose to take one of these captains.
  • Lightning Descent (20pts): . This enhancement can only be placed on a Shield-Captain in Allarus Terminator Armour. It lets this unit make an ingress move turn 1. You can’t get much of a bigger alpha threat in your army than a turn 1 deep strike if that’s something you’re looking to build around.

Stratagems

  • Vigil Unending (2CP): In your Opponent’s Shooting or Fight phase, when an enemy unit targets an Adeptus Custodes Terminator unit, attacks that target your unit have -1 D until that enemy unit has finished their attacks. What’s there to say, this is one of the only 2CP strats in the Custodes codex, but for good reason, damage reduction is pretty good on 6+ wound models.
  • Unleash the Lions (1CP): In your command phase you may select an Adeptus Custodes Terminator Unit that has 2+ models, that unit splits into individual units containing 1 model each and are considered to now have a starting strength of 1. This is a very potent strat that has been around since 8th edition in some form or another but really finds its purpose in this particular codex with the new, improved profiles your Aquillons and Allarus are sporting. 
  • Fury of the Emperor (1CP): During your charge phase when a Custodes Terminator unit that made an ingress move this turn is selected to charge you can give that unit +2 to their charge rolls. Your terminators are gonna be ingressing their hearts out in this Detachment and +2 goes a long way to shoring up your probability issues.

Detachment Combos

There are a number of great synergies you can access with Lions of the Emperor. The new points costs mean that you’re often going to find yourself with far fewer activations than Custodes would have put together in the past, having access to Unleash in these situations lets you triple up on the Mortal Wound and Magna Imperator reroll effects in Emperor’s Chosen or the Battle-Shock tests in Shadowkeepers. Even without, this Detachment is just a solid one if you have any interest in investing in terminators of any variety.

Is It Good?

Allarus, Trajann, and Vexilus Praetor. Credit: Pendulin

For sure! Custodes got faster with this edition but they’re also more compact. Being able to spread your love further and be everything everywhere all at once can’t be bad.

Final Thoughts

While I think there is an initial read of the Custodes Codex that would lend you to look more at standard guard or jet-bikes, the board control and shocking speed of Lions makes it a really exciting Detachment to have in your back pocket.

title: 11th Edition Detachment Focus: Guardians of the Throne
content:
Following hot on the heels of the Emperor’s Angels come his Praetorian Guard. The Adeptus Custodes get an early 11th edition Codex, and with it a slew of new rules and Detachments. In this article, we’re taking a look at the Guardians of the Throne Detachment.

Every 11th Edition Codex comes with an all-rounder 3DP Detachment aimed at providing a solid introduction to the way the faction plays. These have been hit and miss so far, in that there's been one hit for Orks and one miss for Marines. Happily for fans of glorious golden hosts, Guardians of the Throne lands firmly in the hit column, providing a very solid way to start your journey into fielding Custodes.

Thanks to Games Workshop for providing us with a review copy of this Codex and a provisional version of the Munitorum Field Manual. Any rules or points costs we reference are subject to change until they are published on the Warhammer 40K App.

Guardians of the Throne

Detachment Cost: 3 DP

Force Disposition: Priority Assets and Purge the Foe

Guardians is the 3 DP beginner-friendly Detachment in this Codex designed to let you do a little bit of everything with your golden army without having to overthink about pesky things like good unit choices or synergies. Just trundle up and play. On the plus side, this Detachment has access to some great strats and enhancements meaning if you want to keep things simple you don’t end up losing out on too much of the power trying to mix and match the others will get you.

Pendulin's Custodes

Detachment Rule: Martial Mastery

In the Fight Phase when an Adeptus Custodes is selected to Fight, that unit’s melee attacks have either Sustained Hits 1 or Lethal Hits. Current Custodes players will recognize these as the 10th Edition nerfed Ka’tah forms that were the books’ original main rule. Given just how hard and fast every unit in the codex can hit, having access to these is a neat little boon to apply army-wide.

Favored Ka’tah

None. You aren’t running a Shield Host you selfish dingus, you don’t get this cool rule. All Ka’tahs are equal to you.

Enhancements

  • Bane of Abominations (20pts): Adeptus Custodes model only. This model’s attacks that target an enemy Character/Monster/Vehicle have +1 to wound rolls. This is just an excellent enhancement to have with the boosts to the output of the entire gamut of Custodes’ characters.
  • Castellan’s Mark (25pts): Adeptus Custodes model only. Once both players have finished deploying their armies you may select up to 3 units to place into strategic reserves regardless of how many units are already there. Castellan’s Mark has seen a few iterations over the years, all of them with powerful knock-on effects and this one is no exception. Being able to potentially null-deploy your army can be amazing.
  • Eagle’s Eye (30pts): Adeptus Custodes model only. This model has +1 wound and once per battle when attacks are allocated to this model you can improve its invulnerable save to 3+. This is fine but you probably won’t use it.
  • Emperor’s Light (15pts): This weapon can be allocated to an Adeptus Custodes model in your army. It grants them Extra Attacks 3 at WS 2+, Str 5, AP 2 and 2 DMG. When combined with the Sustained Hits from Martial Mastery you can make a pretty brutal one man MEQ wrecking crew if you so desire.

Stratagems

  • Superhuman Focus (1CP): At the end of any phase, select an Adeptus Custodes unit that is not readied and make them readied. There are times when you need to do more than one type of karate in a turn. This lets you do that without stacking expensive Shield Captains throughout your list.
  • Shield of Honour (1CP): At the start of the fight phase when an enemy model engaged with an Adeptus Custodes Infantry/Mounted makes its attacks, if it did not choose to make all of those attacks against that unit then it suffers -1 to hit AND -1 to wound for all of its attacks. Punishing your opponent’s big punchers for not focusing down a single unit is a helluva drug.
  • In Auramite Clad (1CP): When a friendly Adeptus Custodes Unit that is not a Wardens unit is targeted by a shooting attack or in the fight phase, reduce the AP of those attacks by 1. Armour of Contempt on 2+ armour saves is just swell. 
  • Unlimited Endurance (1CP): When a friendly Adeptus Custodes unit ends an advance move they are still eligible to declare a charge and all of their ranged weapons gain the Assault keyword if they did not already have it. Advance + Shoot/Charge on a stick is something you’ll always desire given the low activation count of some of your lists.
  • Prime Target (1CP): In your shooting phase when an Adeptus Custodes unit is selected to shoot, that unit may reroll 1 hit, wound, and damage roll. 3 CP rerolls for the price of 1? That’s a pretty good rate!
  • Swift as the Eagle (1CP): During your opponent’s movement phase when an enemy unit ends its movement within 8" of a friendly unengaged Trusted Sentinel unit. That Trusted Sentinel Unit can make a normal move of d3+3". As always, reactive moves are incredible and the narrow band of it being only on Trusted Sentinels is not that big of a dip. This strat is also found in the Honoured Companions Detachment.

Detachment Combos

None, you can’t do that. It would be cheating.

Is It Good?

Custodian Sentinels. Credit: Pendulin

It’s 3 DP, so while fine, it won't beat out the best combos you can land with other Detachments. But also, it still has some sick stratagems, a decent Detachment rule and a couple of really solid enhancements so it’s ‘good enough’.

Final Thoughts

As far as 3DP Detachments go, Guardians of the Throne is pretty well-designed. If you’re a beginner player that doesn’t want to overcomplicate things and get used to the army you honestly can’t go wrong with this set up. The stratagems are all very useful to amazing and 2 of the enhancements are great to have in your back pocket. The lack of a Favoured Ka’tah and the sheer power of most of the other 1 DP Detachments is the main reason you’ll rarely want to call on this one.

title: 11th Edition Detachment Focus: Null Maiden Vigil
content:
Following hot on the heels of the Emperor’s Angels come his Praetorian Guard. The Adeptus Custodes get an early 11th edition Codex, and with it a slew of new rules and Detachments. In this article, we’re taking a look at the Null Maiden Vigil Detachment.

With Custodes elevated to new but expensive profiles, Sisters of Silence are in the spotlight to provide some glue to hold the army together. If you want to lean in on that plan, Null Maiden Vigil provides some handy augmentations to the Sisters, helping them contribute a few key boosts to the rest of your army. Let’s check it out.

Thanks to Games Workshop for providing us with a review copy of this Codex and a provisional version of the Munitorum Field Manual. Any rules or points costs we reference are subject to change until they are published on the Warhammer 40K App.

Changelog

  • 2026-10-03 (Current): Updated for 11th Edition Codex.
  • 2026-02-18: Original Publication
Detachment Cost: 1 DP

Force Disposition: Disruption

Null Maiden Vigil, obviously, provides buffs purely for the Sisters of Silence, covering a mighty five Datasheets. Make the weird heresy sandworm tank in plastic, cowards. Anyway - the buffs are pretty solid, particularly around inflicting battle-shock, as the horror of the Sisters overwhelms your foes.

Detachment Rule: Silent Sisterhood

Your Anathema Psykana units gain the Creeping Dread aura. This creates a 12” bubble in which enemy units that are either below Starting Strength or are PSYKER units must take a battle-shock test at -1 in the opponent’s Battle-shock step.

Prosecutors also become Battleline, and you can make a Knight-Centura your Warlord.

Enhancements

These are obviously both for Anathema Psykana models only. 

  • Huntress’ Eye (10pts): In your Movement Phase, you can select a visible enemy unit within 12” of this unit, and force them to take a battle-shock test at -1. This is really good - forcing tests at -1 is a generally useful ability, and doing it very early in your turn makes it better, as you can plan around the result. You want to pick what you’re doing with this and pop it off straight away at the start of movement for that reason. Worth noting, also, that while this is a Character enhancement, the enemy only has to be visible to the whole unit, so you can string the Centura back for safety. The price is also very attractive.
  • Oblivion Knight (15pts): The unit gets +1 to hit, or +1 to hit and wound if targeting a battle-shocked or Psyker unit. In theory this is decent on Vigilators, but runs into the issue that the investment for a full squad with a Knight and this is 170pts, only just shy of the cost of two Allarus, which will be better for you a lot of the time even if this detachment is in your army.

Stratagems

Each of the three Sisters units gets a dedicated Stratagem, which gives you some punchy options, but does mean you need to be quite deep on Sisters to get value from all of them.

  • Anathema Blademastery (1CP): Gives Vigilators either Sustained Hits or Lethal Hits. This seems like the best way to go if you want to run 10 of them, as it lets them trade up into a lot of stuff.
  • Psy-Chaff Volley (1CP): After a Prosecutor squad has shot, pick an enemy that was hit to be prosecuted till the end of the turn. Attacks that target them have +1AP. This is the good stuff, and probably your single biggest draw to this Detachment. Jumping Custodian shooting to AP-2 or their melee to AP-3 makes a huge difference in output, and you are actively excited to pop this off. It’s also fine if you’re leaning in hard on the Sisters theme, as it tees up Witchseekers very nicely.
  • Purgation Sweep  (1CP): When Witchseekers shoot in your shooting phase, give their guns either +1A, or +2A if the enemy is a Psyker or Battle-shocked. Realistically, you are very likely to have more exciting ways to spend your CP in most situations as a generalist Custodes build. If you’re really going hard on the Sisters theme, it can be quite good to use a small Purgation unit to (hopefully) set up a bigger one for this by applying battle-shock.

Detachment Combos

The best stuff here is Psy-Chaff Volley and the battle-shock tricks. The latter kind of goes with anything, and the former gets the most benefit if you’re landing lots of attacks on foes. That works especially effectively with either the Aquilian Shield, which can boost up their shooting volume via their Ka’tah and an enhancement, or the Emperor’s Chosen, who hit and wound stuff more. Unit-wise, it also combos pretty well with power talon Terminators, and lists heavy on Terminators will probably need to lean more on Sisters to fill out numbers, so Lions of the Emperor also seems like a plausible combo.

Is It Good?

Anathema Psykana (Sisters of Silence) by Crab-stuffed Mushrooms

This is genuinely quite handy, with some caveats. Pretty much every Custodes build we’ve come up with runs at least two units of Sisters, and if you make both of them Prosecutors, then just Psy-Chaff Volley is helpful (and if you add a Centura to a unit for Huntress’ Eye, even more utility). The downside is that you’ll be giving up access to one Detachment’s worth of buffs for your Custodes.

That isn’t necessarily the end of the world. What we’ve found while building lists is that they’re so small that once you start doubling up on any units, you can end up only really needing one keyword-specific Detachment to buff them (on top of the Shield Host you’re definitely taking). In addition, being able to make a Centura your Warlord is genuinely extremely relevant - Custodes characters whip but they’re not cheap, so having a way to take a 55pt Warlord opens up list design considerably (though losing the bonus CP sucks). The main issue I have with this Detachment is that if you’re a weird sicko who wants to run a full Sisters army, it’s not fantastic for that because the Detachment rule rapidly ends up on diminishing returns. As a bolt-on, though, this is very credible.

Final Thoughts

You’ll certainly be seeing a lot of Sisters in the next few months, and as people iterate on lists, I suspect some people will reach for the flexibility this enables.

title: 11th Edition Detachment Focus: Auric Champions
content:
Following hot on the heels of the Emperor’s Angels come his Praetorian Guard. The Adeptus Custodes get an early 11th edition Codex, and with it a slew of new rules and Detachments. In this article, we’re taking a look at the Auric Champions Detachment.

Every Custodian now packs a profile that makes Characters in other Detachments weep, and their heroes go above and beyond even that. They’ll be few in number, but operate like true gods of battle in the new Codex, and if you want to unleash their fullest potential, the Auric Champions Detachment provides that.

Thanks to Games Workshop for providing us with a review copy of this Codex and a provisional version of the Munitorum Field Manual. Any rules or points costs we reference are subject to change until they are published on the Warhammer 40K App.

Changelog

  • 2026-10-03 (Current): Updated for 11th Edition Codex
  • 2026-02-16: Original Publication
Detachment Cost: 1 DP

Force Disposition: Purge the Foe

Obviously this Detachment primarily enhances the mighty Shield Captains and Blade Champions of the Custodes, but there actually is a fairly powerful Stratagem for everyone else too, so pay attention even if you don’t plan on putting more than your mandatory Warlord pick on the table.

Detachment Rule: Assemblage of Might

In your Command Phase, you can designate one enemy unit as a dreadful foe until your next Command Phase. Your Adeptus Custodes Character models get +1 to Wound against that foe.

This is, obviously, very strong, helping you topple the mightiest foes. It’s especially strong on the Blade Champion, Trajann or the regular Shield Captain, and although the Bike Captain can’t benefit on the charge, it makes their hurricane bolters quite tasty. Because you’re likely to have 3-4 Characters at most, this is also a fair bit easier to use than some similar effects, as it’s usually pretty clear who needs to be hit real hard.

Enhancements

As a Character-focused Detachment, Auric Champions gives you three Enhancement picks rather than two, in exchange for one fewer Stratagem.

  • Shroud of the Hidden Blade (20pts): Gives an Adeptus Custodes model Stealth and Lone Operative. This is pretty great in this Detachment, as being able to take a solo Character with confidence helps squeeze one more into your list. It’s also extraordinarily funny on a bike Captain to create what is, by any other faction’s standards, a high speed flying Lone Op Dreadnought that can zoom a decent way out of range after killing stuff. Also quite good on an Allarus captain because of their teleport shunt, and for both options this Detachment enabling you to reload once-per-game abilities makes it even stronger.
  • Inspirational Exemplar (10pts): Infantry only. Once per battle round, you can un-battle-shock a friendly Custodes unit within 9” at the start of any phase. Custodes are pretty resilient to battle-shock, but with so few units any failure can be a disaster, so for 10pts having this to smooth it out is good.
  • Superior Creation (30pts): Infantry only. At the end of a phase in which this model is destroyed, they stand back up on 3W on a 2+. Now. Obviously this is pretty good, and it’s particularly strong (again) on a solo Allarus. However, the glaring issue here is that this does not, currently, specify once-per-game. Even with how juiced this book is I’m like 90% sure that’s not intentional, but it’s a mark of how big the swings in this one are that there’s still 10% doubt. Hopefully we’ll get a quick FAQ on this one.

Stratagems

  • Gilded Champion (1CP): Once per game, per Character, when they activate a “once per battle, per unit” ability, you can grant them an extra use to store for later on (though they can’t use it again in the same phase). This is very strong, especially for Allarus Captains and Bike Captains. Do note however that you currently can’t use this on Trajann’s Moment Shackle, because that’s “once per battle, per army”, and this specifies “per unit”. The only minor downside of this beyond that is that you have to activate it at the point you use the first activation, so you’re essentially investing a CP rather than getting immediate benefit. Just make sure you don’t close off your short-term goals.
  • Duty Unto Death (1CP): A Custodes unit fights on death on a 3+, with Character models getting +1 to the roll. This is extremely good, and is a complete nightmare for any enemy melee build to try and work around. Quite genuinely, you could end up taking this Detachment even in “normal” lists with just a couple Characters for this and access to Purge.

Detachment Combos

Auric Champions can end up useful in a few situations. First up, if you find yourself leaning in on one category of unit out of regular infantry, bikes and Terminators, you can end up in a situation where you don’t really need a third pick, and the stratagems and Detachment rule here can be enough of a draw.

If you’re aiming for a balanced build, I think Terminators pair best with this, and thus like Lions. If you’re going herohammer, hordes are a potential threat, and talon Aquilons are the best anti-horde tool in the book. Being able to teleport round the table also helps your pieces go further, and tagging the Terminator effects onto Trajann is also great. If you really can’t pick between unit types, you can also just go for Null-Maiden and the Shield Host of your choice, letting you still cram in plenty of Characters, filling out your list with some good scoring.

Alternatively, you can lean in on playing the smallest possible army, in which case there’s a few options. If you crave only gold, I think Emperor’s Chosen, Auric Champions and Might of the Moritoi is pretty awesome, with the EC re-rolls smoothing out your damage output, and solo Characters running amok alongside dreads.pieces.

Is It Good?

Custodes Shield Captain. Credit: NotThatHenryC

Yes, it seems strong. Pretty much all the Detachments in this book do, so that doesn’t make it that special, but there are some uniquely vicious enhancement options here, and some really good Stratagems.

Final Thoughts

Make sure to bring your signature look of superiority whenever your foe challenges your auramite-clad champions.

title: MTG Corn Maze Secret Lair value breakdown
content:
Surprisingly, Magic: The Gathering's latest Secret Lair Superdrop goes extremely hard on Jim Henson's Labyrinth. There's also some classy art deco lands, some stoner treefolk, and Marvel zombies. An eclectic mix.

Below we'll explore all seven Lairs in the Corn Maze Superdrop and see which has the best reprint value.

These Lairs are all being sold for $29.99 or $39.99 for the foils, so that's the baseline we want to see the cards hitting. It's also worth noting you get a Labyrinth-skinned Maze of Ith if you spend over $200. That's a $10 card, if you want to factor it in.

Finally, the usual disclaimer applies. I can't know what the Secret Lair cards will actually sell for on the secondary market, I can only tell you what they're worth now. But this list will hopefully be some use in showing you what's a good deal and what is clearly not.

8. Manufactured Grounds by See Machine

  • Ancient Den - $1.60 Nonfoil / $18.67 Foil
  • Seat of the Synod - $1 Nonfoil / $51.96 Foil
  • Vault of Whispers - $4.59 Nonfoil / $12 Foil
  • Great Furnace - $2.81 Nonfoil / $50 Foil
  • Tree of Tales - $1.16 Nonfoil / $15.16 Foil
  • Total - $11.16 Nonfoil / $147.79 Foil

Most land drops are pretty mid, though WotC has at least upped its offering lately and stopped charging $30 for five basics.

Here we have the cycle of artifact lands, though, once banned in Standard for breaking Affinity, and barred from Modern at the very inception of the format. While it's still a touch annoying that we only get one of each card, these are at least very viable in artifact EDH decks, where you're only allowed one copy anyway.

While they're at the bottom of the list when we look at the cheapest non-foils (it doesn't help that three were recently reprinted in the Edge of Eternities landfall deck) the foil prices give some insight into the true potential here.

That's because there are very few foil printings of these cards (pretty sure it's just Vault of Whispers, which is in the Necron precon). The rest were only printed in foil in other Secret Lairs, lending a look at just how expensive an exclusive full art version of an ubiquitous land can truly become.

7. Artist Series: Veronique Meignaud

  • Bloodsoaked Champion - $0.42 Nonfoil / $2.24 Foil
  • Voldaren Pariah // Abolisher of Bloodlines - $0.59 Nonfoil / $2.27 Foil
  • Ashnod's Altar - $13 Nonfoil / $20 Foil
  • Cabal Stronghold - $12.44 Nonfoil / $22.66 Foil
  • Total - $26.45 Nonfoil / $47.17 Foil

This Artist Series drop showcases Veronique Meignaud's work, full of fluidity and vibrant color. This artist's most famous Magic pieces are probably full art lands, though gamers might also recognize her style from Dishonored.

Anyway, this one sadly falls just short of my $30 minimum. Ashnod's Altar and Cabal Stronghold are both valuable pick-ups, but if Wizards is only going to give us a measly four cards in a drop, it's a bit ridiculous for two of them to cost less than $1.

1/2

6. Through The Labyrinth

  • Timely Ward - $4.16 Nonfoil / $4.16 First Foil printing
  • Chronomantic Escape- $2.70 Nonfoil / $11 Foil
  • Delayed Blast Fireball - $16 Nonfoil / $12.84 Foil
  • Tempt with Discovery - $3.14 Nonfoil / $6.54 Foil
  • Leveler - $4.28 Nonfoil / $4.63 Foil
  • Thran Temporal Gateway - $0.55 Nonfoil / $1.46 Foil
  • Rogue's Passage - $0.45 Nonfoil / $1.80 Foil
  • Total - $31.28 Nonfoil / $42.43 Foil

See? You can do bigger drops, WotC! The card selection for this drop is nearly as terrible as the art is luscious, but with so much included, it's able to just about push past $30. Notably, this drop gives Timely Ward its first foil, and with that included, the foil value hits $40 as well.

While the cards in this drop are mostly not good, don't map particularly  well onto the Labyrinth flavor, and are pretty hard to read, they are very pretty. We can all be thankful Wizards threw in the burn-y red board wipe card Delayed Blast Fireball, which really salvages this Lair.

5. Marvel: Zombies

Unstoppable Slasher - $4.50 Nonfoil / $5.79 Foil
Zombie Apocalypse - $0.70 Nonfoil / $5.54 Foil
Vogar, Necropolis Tyrant - $15 First Nonfoil / $15 Foil
God-Eternal Bontu - $0.40 Nonfoil / $6.42 Foil
Wilhelt, the Rotcleaver - $9.85 Nonfoil / $12 Foil
Varina, Lich Queen - $3.99 Nonfoil / $3.54 Foil
Total -  $34.44 Nonfoil / $48.29 Foil

Vogar, Necropolis Tyrant is the obvious highlight in this batch of creepy Marvel-skinned shamblers. The card was only ever printed in the Game Night box, creating a bizarre situation where it only existed in foil up to now. This is the first regular copy to see print.

Marvel: Zombies follows my favorite trend for Secret Lairs (apart from the return of some form of print-to-demand): all of its cards work well together in the same deck.

You even get a suitable commander with Varina, Lich Queen. Some might find that slightly annoying, since it feels like Varina was only just reprinted as Evil Dead's Linda. But I dunno, I just really like it when WotC provides everything a player with a particular niche interest needs.

If that's you, go my child. Spread your wings and build the Marvel zombie deck of your dreams. Although since almost none of the other Marvel cards work with zombies, I'm not sure what you'll do for the other 94 cards. I guess you're going to have to get really good at proxying.

Hey, at least there's Undead Hand Ninja!

1/2

4. How It's Done

Dawn's Truce - $6.27 Nonfoil / $8.82 Foil
Unbreakable Formation - $0.76 Nonfoil / $1.37 Foil
Freed from the Real - $7.60 Nonfoil / $15 Foil
Swan Song - $11 Nonfoil / $60 Foil
Demonic Counsel - $2.27 Nonfoil / $3.32 Foil
Tempt with Immortality - $1.60 Nonfoil / $1.60 First foil printing
Underworld Breach - $7.48 / $10 Foil
Total - $36.98 Nonfoil / $100.11 Foil

This is the only third-party IP Lair in the superdrop that doesn't rename any of its cards - a mild point in its favor, methinks. With the KPop Demon Hunters drop, we can see the card quality is steadily rising, too. While there are no absolute knockouts, everything here is at least playable, and there are many singles worth more than $5.

If Dawn's Truce hadn't just appeared in a Stardew Valley drop that's selling very cheaply on the secondary market, the foil value of this drop would be even more impressive.

While I give WotC credit for putting in a bunch of strong staples, it seems a missed opportunity that we didn't get any creature cards representing the titular demon hunters.

1/2

3. Should You Need Us

Jodah, the Unifier - $2.95 Nonfoil / $3.29 Foil
Lu Xun, Scholar General - $0.46 Nonfoil / First Foil printing
Kami of the Crescent Moon - $8.05 Nonfoil / $23 Foil
Kogla, the Titan Ape - $3.26 Nonfoil / $3.30 Foil
Shigeki, Jukai Visionary - $0.36 Nonfoil / $0.56 Foil
Wort, Boggart Auntie - $30 Nonfoil / $162 Foil
Total - $45.08 Nonfoil / $192.15 Foil

The Labyrinth drop featuring the 'goodies' has a bunch of reskinned legendary creatures. I guess they could technically all serve under Sarah in a Jodah, the Unifier deck, but it would be pretty terrible. No, you're probably going to want to split them up.

For non-Labyrinth fans, the decision here is quite an easy one: are you in the market for a copy of Wort? This goblin card, only ever printed in original Lorwyn, is worth the asking price all by itself. If you want one, this is a very good deal indeed.

2. Peace, Love, & Treefolk

Dauntless Dourbark - $4.15 / $6.61
Leaf-Crowned Elder - $7.84 / $21.50
Timber Protector - $23.77 / $43.49
Treefolk Harbinger - $6.50 / $17.00
Doran, the Siege Tower - $8.52 / $11.00
Total - $50.78 Nonfoil / $99.60 Foil

The most eyepopping of the Lairs, I'm going to go out on a limb here and say this art will be divisive. Whether you love it or can take or leaf it, this is a great foundation for a Doran treefolk deck, with tons of card value.

The rarest card, Timber Protector, is literally only good in this niche tribe, but it's probably the strongest Treefolk card out there, and in dangerously short supply. In fact, this whole lair has been uprooted from Lorwyn block, which helps to explain the relatively high prices.

1. Fear Me, Love Me

Muxus, Goblin Grandee - $12.00 Nonfoil / $110 Foil
Boggart Shenanigans -$3.50 Nonfoil / $34 Foil
Dance with Calamity - $0.35 Nonfoil / $0.35 First Foil printing
Goblin Rabblemaster - $0.73 Nonfoil / $2.02 Foil
Claim the Firstborn - $0.25 Nonfoil / $0.47 Foil
Trinisphere - $40 / $66 Foil
Total - $56.81 Nonfoil / $215.78 Foil

You might have been wondering where the Goblin King was among all these Labyrinth cards, and now you have your answer: he's got his own six-card drop.

This one features lots of renamed red cards, a mysteriously smooth-crotched Bowie, and… er… the Trinisphere? Okay then. While it doesn't fit with the rest of this goblin Lair at all, it's the most valuable card in the entire superdrop, making it the best of the lot, at least from the cold, hard perspective of monetary value.

A sour note to end on, WotC has included a two-card Rebecca Guay scene with the Sarah card from 'Should You Need Us', trying to entice you to pick up both drops. Not sure I like that idea very much! Perhaps this is why that other drop had the more expensive goblin card, too.

Overall, I was pleased to see how many of these drops had six or more cards, and (if you ignore the land drop) only one fell beneath the $30 minimum. Not bad!

If you want to pick up anything from the Corn Maze Superdrop, head to WotC's SL website on October 12, 8 am PT. You can also share your thoughts on the drop with us over on the Wargamer Discord.
