title: The best board games of 2026
content:
For the last four years, it's been my job to track the top board games releasing each year, test them, and bring you the results. Gathered here are the best board games of 2026 so far, as well as my guide to the all time best board games that live in my head rent-free.

These are the games that did something special to capture my heart. Perhaps they nail a genre so hard that they became a new comfort game. Maybe they're innovative, capable of changing how we think about board games as an art form. Or maybe they're so strategically rich that you could play them over and over and never grow bored.

Why you can trust us ✔ We spend hours testing games, toys, and services. Our advice is honest and unbiased to help you buy the best. Find out how we test.

Below you'll find the best new board games of 2026, followed by a further 40 all time greats split into smaller top 10 lists for different categories.

  • Best board games of 2026
  • Best board games for beginners
  • Best strategy board games
  • Best thematic board games
  • Best board games for families

Best board games of 2026

Half of 2026 has passed us by, and plenty of excellent board games have already appeared. I'm not quite done testing them all - and there's still many more on the way - but these are the best of the year that I've played. I'll be updating this regularly as I get my hands on more of the best 2026 board games, so be sure to come back!

Drillers

By July, Drillers was my board game to beat for 2026. In this deck-builder you play as mech-piloting prospectors boring deep into an abandoned mine in search of wealth and glory. It's immediately full of charm, with each player's custom rustbucket of a mech doing a lot to convey the sense of light-hearted adventure.

The core rules are pretty standard for a deck-builder: you start with a shoddy deck representing the initial state of your mech and over the course of the game you'll upgrade it with extra storage capacity for fuel or ore, better drills, and the ability to move through the ever expanding mine more effectively. It's not revolutionary - it's quite similar to Lost Ruins of Arnak - but it is extremely well crafted, and packed with character.

To learn more about what this game does do differently, check out my very positive Drillers review.

Hanami

Hanami brings a golden oldie back into print for 2026. Reiner Knizia's famed game Samurai is now about tranquil picnics, but it's no less brutal for its makeover. This is still a simple yet compelling game of area majority, where you race to place the most valuable tiles around specific sites.

The new theme is just as effective, and Hanami still has all the polish of a Knizia classic. You can learn to play in 10 minutes and finish a game in under an hour, but it'll take you years to master. That's especially true with this version's all-new second map and special action tiles.

Read more in my full Hanami review.

Dino Racer

Dino Racer is every bit as enthralling a racing game as Hot Streak or Magical Athlete. This snappy sprint to the finish line sees you placing cards to push different dinos forward, then drafting those same cards to show who you're betting on.

Designer Marceline Leiman does so much with a little, and this fast-paced party game is one is bound to get your group laughing and shouting. Expect unexpected upsets, dramatic leads, and plenty of falling at the final hurdle. People keep asking me to bring this one to gatherings, and I'm not surprised.

You can read more in my full Dino Racer review.

World Order

World Order, from the publishers of Hegemony, is one for the strategy lovers. You'll play as a major global power in the real world of the 2010s: America, China, Russia, or the European Union. There are many mechanics that bring this extremely political game to life: resource management, area control, economic trade, deck-building - the list goes on.

It's a complex yet enthralling struggle for victory points. You can expect plenty of analysis paralysis, and tense, hours-long games. That might not be for everyone, but World Order's effective, all-too-real theme makes it a system worth paying extra attention to.

Learn more in our World Order review.

The Two Towers Trick-Taking Game

There are many fantastic board games set in Middle-Earth, but The Lord of the Rings Trick-Taking Game has quickly become one of my favorites. This trilogy of board games (of which the first two have released) retells the entire saga of The One Ring as a co-op trick-taking card game.

Players control one or more key figures from the story, each with their own goals and abilities. You must complete every character's mission to finish the chapter, and as you advance, this becomes ever more challenging. The Fellowship of the Ring and The Two Towers are both thoughtful and frankly gorgeous board games that reward careful cooperation. Seriously, don't skip these.

Read my Two Towers Trick-Taking Game review to learn more.

Viticulture: Bordeaux

This is a bit of a cheeky entry, because the base game already made my 'best of' list further on down. However, Viticulture: Bordeaux is such an immense improvement on the base game that I couldn't ignore it. It's already a strong contender for the best board game expansion of 2026.

It's still a staple worker placement where you're competing to make the most valuable wines, but this version has a much snappier start. It introduces a new expert mechanic and altered turn order rules that make for intriguing, thinky decision-making. Plus, several balancing tweaks make each game closer than ever.

This is one for true lovers of Viticulture who want to see the creases ironed out. Somehow, though, Stonemaier has also managed to make the game more approachable to newcomers by reducing luck elements and balancing out winning strategies.

You can find out more about this essential expansion in my glowing Viticulture: Bordeaux review.

Flip 7 With a Vengeance

Flip 7 is a game I believe everyone should own, however much they like board games. Flip 7 With a Vengeance, the card game's meaner, younger sibling, won't make everyone happy in quite the same way. Some will find the amped up 'take that' mechanics too harsh. I, however, think this is the superior way to play one of the best push-your-luck games around.

Like in the original Flip 7, players are racing to 200 points. Each turn, you'll choose to hit or stick, Blackjack-style, with repeat numbers causing you to bust. This version of Flip 7 comes with even more 'special' cards that let you interact with other players - discarding and swapping their cards, freezing them out of a round, and so on.

The player interaction is constant, and it's brutal. Everyone around the table will be arguing with each other, but when you ask if they want to play again, it's an enthusiastic 'yes'.

Learn more in my Flip 7 With a Vengeance review.

Cozy Stickerville

Cozy Stickerville is the Stardew Valley of board games (yes, even though there's a literal Stardew Valley board game). You inherit a rural patch of land from your father, and it's up to you to build a thriving town - all made up of charming stickers. That's right, this is a legacy game.

Each turn, you'll draw a card from this year's event deck. Then you can perform one action found on a sticker or card in play. Perhaps you'll search mines for gold, go on dates with a villager, or plant flowers by the roadside.

With five different endings, this is a game all about choices and their consequences. Will you build a thriving, money-hungry metropolis, or will you keep the landscape idyllic and rural? The narrative isn't very complex, but the act of making a permanent mark on the board is as enthralling as it is charming.

Sanibel

Wingspan's Elizabeth Hargrave has a knack for turning the natural world into a chill board game experience, and she's done it again with Sanibel. The soothing set collection game about sweeping a beach for sea shells hasn't bested Wingspan in my eyes, but I'm a big fan nonetheless.

Players take turns striding up and down the shore, picking up pretty shells for their personal player board. The shells slot into spaces on your board as if you'd stuffed them in your bag. The type and position of your shells matters hugely for scoring, so choose wisely from the sands!

I love a solitaire-like tile puzzler, with Azul and Harmonies being firm favorites in my home. Sanibel shares a lot of with these style of games, and I can see it being a hit with families and hobbyists alike.

Threaded

Threaded: A Game of Needles and Points is both cozy and cutthroat. You'll play as needleworkers completing bargello commissions, and the most successful business wins the day.

Gameplay-wise, this is a worker placement where the early bird gets the best choice of threads, patterns, and tools. You'll need to thread fabric onto your needle before you can complete a pattern, and this unique mechanic turns Threaded into a thoughtful strategic puzzle, though one that's still friendly to beginner board gamers.

Learn more in my full Threaded review.

Tenby

Board game release dates are a funny thing. Tenby technically came out in 2025, but it didn't hit retail properly until 2026. All I know is that I love this little city-building card game, and I want to shout about it.

Each turn, you'll draft new cards to add to a street in the Welsh coastal town of Tenby. That might be a notable landmark, a terraced house, a piece of pier, or a resident. All have unique scoring powers, and the puzzle is placing cards so they capitalize on the key features of the cards around them. Clouds, benches, birds, and flower pots can all mean big points, if you're organized enough.

It's quick, soothing, and extremely wholesome. The only player interaction is the struggle for cards in the public display, but if you don't mind a solo-ish drafting puzzle, this should be right up your seaside street.

You can find my full review of Tenby here.

Wingspan Pocket

Wingspan Pocket takes Elizabeth Hargrave's beloved engine-building card game reduces the amount of grey matter and table space you need to dedicate to playing it.

Just like regular Wingspan, each player builds up a tableau of gorgeous bird cards, each with unique powers that will trigger when you expand your nest. There are still combos to be found, but you'll only collect six birds across the whole game, reducing the complexity of the interactions between cards while making each choice more important.

Though strategy fans will likely prefer the eagle-sized original, this plucky sparrow is much better suited for families and  filler games.

Check out my my complete Wingspan Pocket review to learn more.

Night at the Zoo

Simple yet enthralling, Night at the Zoo sees you herding lost animals back to their enclosures. Three species start out at the borders of an empty grid, and you'll draft terrain tiles with action symbols to steer them home. It's a delightful little head-scratcher, though the strategic elements are approachable enough for any game-savvy family member.

SETI designer Tomáš Holek flies his euro-loving flag high here. Night at the Zoo is a solitaire-like game with a vast web of decision points. Each animal has a unique way of moving and scoring, and both player boards and tiles introduce new sources of points. It's adorable, and it's compelling. I keep coming back to it.

You can learn more in my full Night at the Zoo review.

Best board games for beginners

I want to make it clear: these aren't the best board games for beginners because they're easy. The entries here are just as engaging as any big-box strategy game with a billion minis. Instead, this mini-list recommends the games you should head for first if you want to get the best idea of what the modern board game hobby is. These approachable entries introduce you to key mechanics, and they're an important part of board gaming history.

Catan

First released in 1995, Catan has survived and thrived for decades. Players compete to dominate an island by building settlements near key resources - grain, ore, wool, lumber, and brick - so they can rake in cards every turn and spend them on expanding their empire.

Things start off benign, but there's only room on this little island for one player to build the roads, cities, and extra buildings they need to win, so it gets competitive fast.

Because it's so simple, it's incredibly easy to go from not knowing the game at all to keenly working out your tactics and plotting how to outmaneuver your rivals. Strategy aficionados may sneer at Catan, but this famous game has a place in every collection - especially if your board gaming journey is just beginning.

Read Wargamer Tim's Catan review to learn more.

Ticket to Ride

Ticket to Ride is many gamer's entry into the tabletop hobby, and for good reason. Simple yet surprisingly drama-filled, Ticket to Ride offers just enough strategy to dip your toe (or sink your teeth) into. The core premise is simple: collect train cards with matching colors and play them to claim a particular route on the map.

While everyone is vying for the longest route, each player also has a secret series of city-to-city journeys they must map to score points. To begin with, Ticket to Ride is calming and non-confrontational, but as the map grows crowded, competition quickly starts to heat up as you race to cut your friends off from their favored routes. It's a delicious tension hidden beneath a whimsical, colorful surface.

Read card-game king Matt's Ticket to Ride review to learn more.

Pandemic

Few co-op games match the 2008 smash hit Pandemic, which nails team-based gameplay so damn hard that I'm still playing over a decade later. In this game, four deadly, brightly colored diseases have each simultaneously infected a large part of the world map. Every turn, the diseases will spread quickly across the planet, and - as a team - you must plan out your limited actions to contain their growth and develop cures for all four as quickly as possible.

Be warned: while the rules aren't complicated, the game can be a genuine challenge, you'll have to learn to make the most of all your characters' abilities in combination with each other, while racing against disease outbreaks that can come at any time. Luckily, working together to achieve that is endlessly satisfying, and Pandemic is a genuine thrill every time we play.

Read more in Wargamer Tim's full Pandemic review.

Carcassonne

Carcassonne is the oldest board game in my collection, and I'll never get rid of it. It's like the perfect sandwich: quick, simple, balanced - yet surprisingly spicy.

In more literal terms, it's a tile-laying game where you'll take turns adding a random tile to an ever-expanding, Medieval French landscape. Place your tile with care, and you can construct lengthy roads, sprawling cities, cozy priories, or lush farmland. These can then be claimed by a colorful meeple from your supply.

Here's where the spice comes in. With enough passive-aggressive turns, multiple meeples will be bickering about who controls a particular road or city. What begins as a calm laying of land becomes a bitter struggle for territory. I've had many arguments over the lay of the land in Carcassonne, and I've loved it every time. Simple, brutal, and effective.

Read my Carcassonne review to learn more.

Azul

Azul is all about placing clack-y mosaic tiles in the most aesthetically pleasing - and highest-scoring - pattern. Each player has their own board, which they want to fill up with certain combinations of mosaic tiles. To obtain these, you'll take turns drafting from tile pools.

Drafting one color means you must take all matching tiles from that pool. These are then placed in a row beside your mosaic, which must be filled with matching tiles before one can be added to the final piece (and scored). But draft carefully, as any tiles you don't have room for spill over and become minus points.

The gameplay loop is oddly soothing, but the strategy hidden underneath quickly grows competitive. Half the fun is the cutthroat act of drafting the exact tile you know an opponent needs.

Read editor Alex' Azul review to learn more.

Wingspan

Wingspan is as satisfying as it is stunning. It's a surprisingly soothing engine-builder that sits perfectly between gateway game and intense strategy session. In Wingspan, you're aiming to attract as many beautiful birds to your habitat as possible. Gather bird cards, collect food, lay eggs, and spend your precious resources to build those birdies nests in the right habitats.

Many birds offer unique powers that, once they've been played, trigger when you perform other resource-gathering actions. Your board grows more powerful over time, and an efficient player can fill their entire board with point-scoring birds by the end-game. Specialize carefully, and you can craft some immensely valuable engines that'll have your opponents all a-flutter.

Read card-game guru Matt's Wingspan review to learn more.

Dominion

Dominion was the first major deck-building board game, and, in my opinion, it's still the best one. The premise doesn't take much explaining. Everyone starts with the same basic deck of cards, which they'll draw from to play cards each turn. Earn money, and you can buy unique cards from the market to modify your deck on future turns. Create enough money-earning combos, and you can start buying valuable plots of land worth victory points.

Dominion accommodates multiple gameplay styles, from the endless turn loop to 'take that!' curses that debuff opposing decks. No two decks ever quite play the same, and that's before you factor in Dominion's many expansions. This is an excellent introduction to a mechanic that changed the face of board gaming as we know it.

Scout

Scout is a smart, quick-playing card game that delights the eye and tickles the brain by twisting trick-taking on its head. On the surface, it resembles classic playing card games like Rummy or Whist. Collect or play cards on your turn to create matching or sequential sets of numbered cards. Points are up for grabs for emptying your hand first, or when other players add one of your previous plays to their hand.

Sounds simple, but there's a twist. You can't change the orientation or order of cards in your hand, so if you want to play a set that could win you the round, you've got to cluster those cards together first. This means you're not just playing against your opponents; you're also fighting the cards you're holding, trying to plan ahead to get the big plays you need.

Learn more in my full Scout review.

7 Wonders

7 Wonders is a real crowd-pleaser, a strategic drafting board game that's truly absorbing, whatever level of board game experience you have. Each player competes to craft the most advanced ancient civilization. Across three ages, you'll draw a hand of cards and, simultaneously with other players, draft a card from it to play. Your hand passes on, and your neighbors then get a chance to grab any value you left behind.

Points come from many sources, whether it be your military might, your coffers of coin, your scientific advancements, or the wonder of the world you gradually build on your player board. Specialization is tempting, but the player who efficiently excels in every area tends to win the day.

The Quacks of Quedlinburg

The Quacks of Quedlinburg is a chaotic push-your-luck game where bravery could net you big wins - or blow up in your face. Its subtly thoughtful design choices mean no bout of bad luck is ever too punishing, and the thrills of a well-played round will fill a room with energy. Better yet, it's simple enough that players of any age can enjoy it.

In Quacks, everyone takes their turn at the same time. You'll randomly draw chips from a bag to add to your swirling cauldron, hoping for the most valuable picks that will increase the points and cash you can claim. But if you pull too many white tokens from your bag, the concoction explodes, severely limiting your yield for that round.

Between brewing sessions, everyone will have a chance to spend their hard-earned money on new, more useful chips for their ingredients bag. With so many changing variables, Quacks of Quedlinburg is anyone's game to run away with - the question is, how much are you willing to bet on your brew?

Read deck building expert Matt's Quacks of Quedlinburg review.

Best strategy board games

Maybe you're someone who delights in a plan well-placed. Perhaps your favorite part of gaming is crunching numbers or carrying out grand, multiple-turn strategies. Maybe words like 'eurogame' or 'crunch' or 'six-hour play time' get you hot under the collar. Or perhaps you've graduated from our list of beginner games, and you're looking to try something with a bit more complexity. Whatever your reasons, these are the mid-to-heavy strategy board games worth checking out.

Arcs

One-part space wargame and one-part trick-taking game, Arcs is a compact yet complex experience, where every turn can dramatically change the tide of play. New players may succumb to analysis paralysis thanks to Arcs' immense, interlocking systems. However, once you've understood its mechanics, Arcs is as tense and exciting as any space opera.

Everything you do in Arcs is determined by the cards you are dealt. The suits decide what actions you can take in a round, from aggressive movement and combat to careful construction jobs. The value of your card decides how much influence you have in the great space race - the highest-value card played lets its player take the maximum possible actions, leaving opponents to best their number or take a turn with reduced efficiency.

Players can also sacrifice the value of their card to declare an ambition. You lose your lead in the race, but playing an ambition you're likely to achieve is a great way to score points. Stockpile resources to score end-of-round points, and you're even more likely to steal an extremely gratifying win.

Learn more in Matt's Arcs review.

Ark Nova

Ark Nova is a surprisingly realistic depiction of what it's like to manage a zoo. Over the course of an hour or two, you'll fill an empty hex grid with animal enclosures and concession stands that increase your appeal to visitors. Entertainment is only one part of zoo management, though, so you'll also need to juggle sponsorships and conferences to further your conservation work.

This is a complex, crunchy strategy game, so you'll need to juggle a range of mechanics to achieve your goals. Actions that change power levels, worker placement, hand management, and drafting all make up the rich tapestry of Ark Nova. It's highly rewarding, but it can be brutal too - it's totally possible to end the game with negative points.

Read the Ark Nova review by Wargamer Tim - who has a personal connection to the zoo industry - to learn more.

Brass: Birmingham

Brass: Birmingham is the ultimate game of industrial expansion, the kind of game that reveals more of its strategic intricacies with every game. You'll play as a titan of British industry, shepherding the city of Birmingham through two of its biggest trade revolutions: canals and railways.

Victory points are awarded to industry moguls who sell the most quality merchandise and build the best transport connections between their manufacturers. This is a through-and-through eurogame, so all other actions, from selling coal and iron at market to taking out loans, are in aid of streamlining and empowering your industrial machine.

Every action counts here. As businesses grow, the map gets more crowded, and you'll soon find yourself making reluctant partnerships with - or deliberately screwing over - your direct competitors. It's an enthralling machine that, while you may struggle to grasp all its moving parts at first, is a joy to watch whirr.

War of the Ring

An hours-long tactical epic, the War of the Ring recreates Middle-earth's historic clash between the Free Peoples and Sauron's armies.

The Free Peoples race to muster political support and troops to overwhelm the armies of shadow, or at least hold them at bay long enough for Frodo and Sam to get the ring to Mount Doom. Meanwhile, the side of shadow hunts the ringbearer, hoping to corrupt him entirely or destroy the armies of good to clinch the win. All the action is resolved with tide-turning dice rolls and well-played event cards.

It's about as tense as a head-to-head can get, and though the rules are comprehensive and complex, it never feels like a slog. It helps a lot that this feels like such a faithful, thematic recreation of the events of The Lord of the Rings - even if your versions of these armies handle things slightly differently.

The Old King's Crown

The Old King's Crown is, according to Wargamer editor Alex,"the most captivating board game I've ever played". He will not stop going on about it.

The Old King's Crown combines whip-smart pacing, beautifully balanced strategy, and a gorgeous fantasy theme. It's a tapestry woven from all manner of board game genres, though its core loop is as simple as it gets: players lay down cards, and the highest number wins.

Each round, you'll play three of these card clashes, aiming to rack up victory points. But in order to win (and keep winning) clashes, you've also got to play the wider strategy game: a scrumptious, layered lasagna of deck-building, engine-building, worker placement, and bluffs galore. Every decision counts, and The Old King's Crown keeps you captivated until the very end.

Read editor Alex's The Old King's Crown review to learn more.

Scythe

Scythe is a chunky strategy game that combines eurogame-style engine-building with some good-old-fashioned territory control. You're thrown into an alternate, sci-fi version of 1920s Eastern Europe, and you'll act as one of several factions that want to dominate the continent.

The way to do that? Control the most territory, construct buildings, beat up other mechs with your mechs, achieve secret objectives, hoard natural resources, and make sure your popularity score is high enough to multiply the value of other point sources. Add in faction-specific abilities and randomized player boards, and you've got plenty of strategy to chew on.

Scythe has a bit of a pacing problem at times, and it'll take strategy game newbies a while to master juggling all of its victory conditions. However, at the right player count, it's a puzzle well-worth investigating.

Read more in my full Scythe review.

Root

Root is the board game that convinced me to love wargames, and it's absolutely because I was sucked in by the adorable animal factions. This is an asymmetric, faction-based game of battle and area control where woodland creatures fight to claim control of their local forest. It's as cute as it is cutthroat.

Each animal faction offers a different playstyle and a unique way to win victory points. While the Marquise de Cat races to gather resources and construct buildings, the Eyrie Dynasties harvest points from an elaborate engine-building exercise. The Woodland Alliance starts with no board presence, but they can tear another faction apart from within by sparking rebellion. Meanwhile, the Vagabond is just a silly little racoon, trading items and siding with whoever seems strongest at the time.

That's before we throw any of the expansion factions in. With so many ways to play, Root rewards a gamer that is willing to return to its woodlands over and over, picking up different tricks along the way. It's strategically rich, it's thematic, and it's gorgeous to look at.

SETI: Search for Extra Terrestrial Intelligence

SETI is as gorgeous as space board games get, but it's more than just a pretty box with a rotating solar system. It's quickly become my favorite eurogame of all time, and the Space Agencies expansion only adds to the yes-ness.

Your ultimate goal is to discover alien life, but because this is a strategy game, your ultimate ultimate goal is to net the most points while doing so. That means landing on planets, scanning the stars, researching new tech, and upgrading your player board all the while to make each action more efficient. Aliens are cool, but you know what's cooler? End-game bonuses.

This is a modern euro that respects your time and isn't afraid to throw a bit of pizazz in with fancy components. Honestly, I don't have a bad word to say about it. A must-play for euro fans, and still worth checking out if complex points salads aren't usually your thing.

Read more in my SETI review.

Viticulture

Viticulture is an approachable mid-weight eurogame, perfect for newcomers to the genre as well as seasoned veterans. It's a pure economic worker placement that tasks you with managing the best vineyard in all of Tuscany. That means planting and growing grapes to later bottle as premium wine of all kinds, as well as giving guided tours of your blossoming business.

You and your rival vineyards must compete for action spaces in order to further your goals, with rewards available for the first worker that completes an action. The actions available change with the weather, so it's important to pay close attention to the seasons. Build structures, fulfill wine orders, and expand just enough that your profit margins are more impressive than everybody else's. It's a thoughtful (and, dare I say, elegant) game that doesn't outstay its welcome.

Make sure you check out 2026's Bordeaux expansion, because it's genuinely transformational.

A Feast For Odin

A Feast For Odin is a worker placement with so many actions to take that it's easy to get overwhelmed by choice. You'll play as Vikings, but you'll do far more than raid and pillage. Your main goal is to stock your settlement (your personal player board) with goods and resources. These generate income, but you'll need to farm (or, yes, raid) to fill your coffers.

Overcome the initial learning curve, and you'll find this is a tile-based, engine-building board game stuffed with interesting decisions and multiple ways to win. If you're good at arranging and optimizing, and you're willing to take a few risks, you're onto a winner.

Best thematic board games

The term 'thematic' covers many board game genres, because it's less about the mechanics and more about the atmosphere they create. These games' rules might perfectly capture the spirit of their concept, or they might create tension in a way no other board game can. Some are simple, quick affairs, while others take over your life for months at a time. All are brilliant.

Blood on the Clocktower

My favorite board game of all time, Blood on the Clocktower is a rich, strategic, innovative take on the tried-and-tested social deduction board game. It marries cheeky bluffing antics and complex mechanics in a way that'll please casual party game lovers and fans of brain-warping strategy board games. It's pricier than other social deduction games on the market, but there really is nothing else like it out there.

In Blood on the Clocktower, everyone has a secret power, role, and alignment. Someone is a demon who, with some aid from their minions, kills innocent townsfolk at night, when everyone has their eyes squeezed shut.

During the day, it's up to the good team to investigate, querying their neighbors and choosing who to execute as the sun goes down. Kill the demon, and good prevails! But allow the murders to go on for two long, and evil will eventually outnumber the villagers - and put an end to them all. Tense and silly in equal measure, this is an addictive, replayable gem that more than justifies its luxury price.

Read more in my Blood on the Clocktower review.

Frosthaven

Gloomhaven's younger yet bigger brother, Frosthaven is an expansive dungeon-crawling RPG that needs hours of commitment to complete. It's an adventure worth embarking on, though, as few board games can match the challenge, immersion, and satisfaction it offers.

When you're not building a snowy base, you'll hop from dungeon to dungeon, fending off seemingly endless combinations of monsters. Objectives are varied, and loot is always on the table, which is handy for all that base-building you'll be doing. Your actions are decided by two cards played each turn, one with its top action resolving and the other its bottom. Combat damage is also determined by cards rather than dice, a eurogame-inspired design choice that reduces randomness and makes this puzzle of efficiency even more strategic.

Read my Frosthaven review to learn more.

The Lord of the Rings: Fate of the Fellowship

Though their themes couldn't be more different, The Lord of the Rings: Fate of the Fellowship shares a lot of DNA with Matt Leacock's previous masterpiece, Pandemic. In this thematic co-op, everyone has control of two famous Fellowship, and you'll use them and their unique powers to fend off enemy forces at key locations. All the while, you must conceal Frodo from the watchful Eye of Sauron and his Nazgûl buddies.

It's an excellent recreation of what makes Tolkien's original story so tense and exciting. Plus, it makes Pandemic's well-worn, decade-old gameplay feel fresh again.

Betrayal at House on the Hill

Betrayal at House on the Hill isn't the most balanced game, but no game has ever captured the haunted house theme as well. You'll play as Scooby-Gang-style teens exploring a creepy abode, taking turns to lay procedural rooms, pick up items, and witness sPoOoOoOky events. The house grows as you go, and when it gets fat enough, it begins to hunger for something new - your lives.

Eventually, a Haunt will begin, and the specific layout of the house determines what storyline you discover. Your team gains a new objective, which usually involves escaping the place with your lives. Someone also tends to turn traitor thanks to a sudden ghostly possession/bout of madness/encounter with a haunted realtor. Betrayal at House on the Hill hits every genre of schlocky horror, and the stories it tells are always hugely exciting.

Read more in my Betrayal at House on the Hill review.

Vantage

Vantage is an immersive choose-your-own adventure game about the joys of exploration. Players crash-land on different parts of a faraway planet, and they must describe their unique perspective as they take different journeys across its landscape.

Your turns focus on performing a variety of evocative actions at each location you visit, with dice rolls determining how taxing they are for your health, morale, and time. Vantage is stuffed with gorgeous art and delicious secrets to uncover, and each playthrough feels a little different.

A lack of win conditions and unusual pacing mean that Vantage won't be everyone's cup of tea. But for me, it's an innovative, meditative experience that I keep coming back to.

Learn more in my full Vantage review.

Spirit Island

Spirit Island is a co-op where an island's elemental spirits must work together to repel eager human colonizers. It turns a classic board game theme on its head in a way that's innovative, emotive, and downright enjoyable to play.

Each turn, everyone plays a power card simultaneously. Move quickly, and you can shake the earth and shape the seas before the invaders spread, but slower, more careful movements will need time to set up. The invaders will expand across the island, but you'll grow in power, too, unlocking new ways to heal the fear and blight these people bring. Victory sees you successfully scare the invaders off the island, but if you're overwhelmed by blight, time, or attacks on a spirit, the colonizers seize the land for good.

Molly House

Molly House is an elegant, thematic game about joy, love, and persecution. You'll play as 18th-century Mollies, LGBTQ+ Londoners looking to throw parties, do a bit of shopping, hook up, and - most importantly - evade the law. Molly House can be fiddly at first, but its strategy and theme soon unfold like the plot of a dramatic novel.

It starts out as a co-op trick-taking game, where everyone cruises London, picking up beaus and earning reputation. Parties are thrown constantly, and everyone contributes cards to the trick-taking game to score as much joy as possible. Before long, though, threats arrive on the scene, and the Mollies must choose to fight for their community's joy - or turn traitor and expose their former friends.

You can learn more in my full Molly House review.

Sky Team

Sky Team is the best two-player board game on the market right now. Thematic and tense, it tasks you and a co-pilot with landing a plane. The task requires hair-trigger precision, careful planning, and some very lucky rolls in your personal pool of dice. It's these dice, rolled at the start of each round, that are spent to flip switches, fire the engines, and keep the plane level. Some values can only be used for certain tasks, while other tasks must be performed in the correct order.

That's a lot of constraints, but there's one big one I haven't mentioned yet. Once the dice are rolled, you and your co-pilot cannot speak. Each player's private pool of dice is secret, so you must use pre-roll planning and intuition to make sure each task gets done on time. Slip up once, and the plane crashes - game over. Sky Team is the ultimate compatibility test, and it's an exhilarating exercise in cooperation.

Learn more in my full Sky Team review.

Sherlock Holmes: Consulting Detective

Sherlock Holmes: Consulting Detective is a compelling and immersive whodunnit that puts an interesting spin on mystery board games. Each case that the esteemed (and slightly condescending) Sherlock sets you plays like a choose-your-own-adventure book.

Examine your evidence, and pick a lead to follow, turning to the relevant page of your case book. This contains interrogations and investigations to read aloud, so the twists and turns of the mystery unfold organically. A thorough examination of the facts will be rewarded by the truth. However, there's an (in our eyes, optional) element of time pressure here too, as Sherlock is far more impressed by sleuths who solve the case in as few moves as possible.

Read my Sherlock Holmes: Consulting Detective review to learn more.

Twilight Imperium

One of the beefiest board games there is, Twilight Imperium offers the perfect balance of theme and strategy. You'll need to invest an entire day if you want to play, but your reward is a vast, varied space opera, with tense negotiations, tight battles, and endless strategic decisions to make.

You'll act as one of 17 space factions looking to dominate the galaxy. Mechanically, that means being first to gain 10 victory points. Many of these are gained through objective cards, but the requirements could include mastering anything from spaceship skirmishes to inter-faction trade. Each faction has unique abilities, and the board is modular, so Twilight Imperium never plays quite the same. It could be the only game you own, and you'd never run out of fresh experiences.

Best board games for families

The best family board games can be enjoyed by players of any age. Don't discount this list if you're old enough to drink! Instead, consider it an arsenal of games to get your children, cousins, parents, or grandparents involved in your favorite hobby. Many of them are also perfect for parties, where an easy yet enticing game is most appealing. These games are simple in the most delightful of ways, and that often means they're addictive.

Flip 7

Flip 7 doesn't have a compelling theme, and it doesn't take much strategy to win. It can be taught in seconds, and games rarely last longer than 20 minutes. Despite all of this, it was one of my favorite games of 2024. A push-your-luck card game that innovates just enough on Blackjack, it's as moreish as a pack of premium cookies.

Flip 7's deck is made up of numbered cards. There's one 'zero' card, one 'one' card, two 'two' cards, three 'three' cards…all the way up to 12 '12' cards. These are shuffled, and each player is presented with the classic gamble: hit or stay. You can pull as many cards as you like, but if you ever draw two cards of the same value, you've gone bust. A handful of special ability cards might save you (or screw over another player), but otherwise, your fate dangles tantalizingly, totally at the mercy of the cards.

Codenames

Codenames turns a simple word association exercise into a nail-biting game of espionage. Two teams of spies must correctly identify their allied agents, each of which hides behind a bizarre codename. Only the team's spymaster knows their true locations, and they can only drop hints in the form of single-word, single-number clues. Does "Garden, 2" point to "carrot" and "green", or could "spade" be on the cards?

It's a race that rewards careful, cautious clues, but there's more than enough room for Codenames to get silly. This ultra-simple word game has, in some hobbyists' eyes, been replaced by the more recent game, Decrypto. I, however, will always turn to Codenames when I want to introduce family and friends to my favorite hobby. It's quick, easy, and never gets old.

Read Wargamer Tim's Codenames review to learn more.

Bomb Busters

Bomb Busters was the most explosive board game of 2024, and not just because it's about defusing bombs. This is a co-op limited communication game that I'd compare most closely to Guess Who, but there's far more strategy under the hood than the iconic children's game.

Everyone plays an adorable bunny bomb buster, each with a row of numbered wires placed in front of them. You can't reveal your row to another bunny, but all wires must be cut to save the city from destruction. How do you achieve such an impossible task? Sweat, logic, and a few lucky guesses. You get a small slither of info to work with, plus some handy equipment to help. Each new mission ups the complexity, but it's nothing you can't handle! Right?

Read my Bomb Busters review to learn more.

Kingdomino

Kingdomino is a charming, colorful take on the classic tile-laying game it shares (half) a name with. You'll play as a monarch looking to expand their kingdom, and you'll score points for ruling over the richest, most diverse terrain possible.

To do that, you'll need to draft domino tiles. Each tile has two different terrain squares, and you'll mainly score points by connecting matching terrain squares. Tiles with crows on should also be a top priority, as they're needed to score - and multiply the scores of - different terrains.

A game of Kingdomino is over in 15 minutes, but you'll often be reaching for a second or third game. It's a moreish morsel that's ideal for introducing younger gamers to the hobby.

Learn more in Wargamer Tim's Kingdomino review - ably assisted by his daughter.

Jaipur

Jaipur is a compact two-player game where careful card management can earn you all the riches in Rajasthan. Two merchants compete to buy and sell the most tantalizing stock at their market stall.

Doing so is deceptively simple. On your turn, you can either add goods to your hand or discard a group of matching cards to earn a valuable token. Each good has a different market value, so you'll need to draft at the perfect time if you want to beat your competitors to the best products. The horde of camels that take up space in the market, too, can be a blessing or a curse, depending on when you add them to your personal herd.

For such a simple game, there's a surprising amount of strategy to mull over. It's a solid introduction to board games at large, and it's always an entertaining use of half an hour.

Read card game expert Matt's Jaipur review to learn more.

Hot Streak

CMYK's Hot Streak is a sensational racing game that's as whimsical as it is somewhat unsettling to look at. This game goes all in on its status as a toy. Four 3D mascot runners, each delightfully more garish than the last, to place on a race track that rolls out of the box.

This is a simple betting game, where everyone takes turns drafting a bet for one of three races. Everyone also gets the chance to throw cards into the action deck, which determines how the runners will behave during the race. That naturally includes charging forward, but it also includes turning around, crashing into other competitors, falling over, or veering off the race course completely (and getting disqualified). Hilarity ensues so hard that you'll often forget that the point of playing is to win the most money.

Learn more in my Hot Streak review.

Harmonies

Harmonies is as soothing as competitive board games get. You're the steward of a landscape that wants to attract as many gorgeous animals as possible. To do that, you'll need to build the right terrain for them, whether that be trees, rivers, mountains, fields, or buildings. Attracting the most animals is a sure way to victory, but each piece of terrain offers a unique, additional way to score.

Each turn, you'll draft an animal card and/or a pool of three terrain tiles. These wooden pieces stack satisfyingly on top of each other to create more valuable landmarks. It's a thoughtful, tactile, somewhat solitary experience - so relaxing that, when everyone totals their final scores, winning feels like a bonus rather than the sole goal.

Read my Harmonies review to learn more.

One Night Ultimate Werewolf

This is the best board game you can play in just 10 minutes. It's a mini game of social deduction, where players are assigned hidden roles and must question each other to uncover the hidden werewolf. Or, if they are the werewolf, they must bluff long enough to get someone else accused of their werewolf-y crimes.

It takes only a few minutes for the shouting and finger-pointing to begin. One Night Ultimate Werewolf is simple, but it's deliciously addictive. A handful of unique role powers throw even more chaos into the mix, swapping roles or giving certain players information at 'night', when everyone has their eyes shut. This is one I've played over and over for years, with various numbers of players, and I never get bored.

Learn more in my One Night Ultimate Werewolf review.

Monikers

Monikers is a quirky take on the classic party game Celebrities, where you must describe something well-known to your team without naming it outright. This version turns that age-old formula on its head by giving you some of the strangest prompts we've ever seen, from Cthulhu to 'The lady who spilled coffee on herself at Mcdonalds'.

The first round plays out like a standard Celebrities game, but in the second round, each team must work with the exact same set of prompts - only with a single word. Round three is rinse and repeat, but you must now mime everything to your team, who'll need to use a combination of memory and confused squinting to work out what you're getting at. It's simple, it's silly, and it's perfect for a casual game night.

Skull

Another board game you could play on your lunch break, Skull is a snappy bluffing game that throws in some bidding mechanics for extra spice. It's a simple card game that has no right to be as engaging as it is, but it's one of my go-to games for parties, quick gaming sessions, or beginner-friendly game nights.

Everyone is handed a pile of cards that look like rock bar beer mats, some decorated with flowers and others with skulls. Players place one to two cards face-down in front of them, and then, someone starts the bid, guessing how many flowers they think are hidden among the cards played. Bidding increases until all players have bid or pass. The highest bidder must then reveal cards, in any order, equal to their bid. If any skulls are flipped, that player loses a card from their pool, but if it succeeds they can flip their flower mat. Flip that mat twice, and you win!

Whew, that was a lot of board games. How many have you played? Are any of your favorites missing? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord.

title: Games Workshop Accidentally Leaks New Dwarf Faction for Age of Sigmar
content:
Games Workshop has a new dwarf faction headed to Age of Sigmar — and we know that because the company accidentally showed it off early.

The Khazalite Holds briefly appeared on the Irish version of the Warhammer Store website before being hastily taken down. GW hasn’t released high-resolution versions of the images, so for now fans are squinting at blurry screenshots. The company also hasn’t commented further on the leak itself.

What We Know So Far

Age of Sigmar already has two duardin factions — the steampunk air pirates of the Kharadron Overlords and the slayer-inspired Fyreslayers — but neither scratches the itch for classic Warhammer dwarves. The Khazalite Holds look set to change that.

The leaked images showed off three distinct groups of miniatures:

  • Footsoldiers — Stoic, unrelenting infantry with shields bearing traditional runes that Warhammer Fantasy veterans will recognise
  • Golem-like constructs — A trio of heavy hitters, described by one observer as “stout as all hell,” armed with greathammers and looking every bit the linebreakers
  • A leader — Thick armour, well-plaited hair, a billowing cloak, a great axe, and an impressive headpiece. Plus a tactical rock, naturally.

The models feature pseudo-Nordic knotwork and runic designs straight out of the Old World, but with the proportions and round bases that Age of Sigmar players are used to.

GW Responds to the Leak

Rather than waiting for Friday’s Big Autumn Warhammer Preview, GW leaned into the leak and shared a bit more about the faction.

“Meet a Gholem of Gazul,” the company said. “What’s a Gholem? Who is Gazul? Well, for now all we can say is that it marches to war amidst the war throngs of the Khazalites Holds – an all-new Duardin faction for Warhammer Age of Sigmar. We’ll delve into the lore, rules and even more sweet new miniatures on Friday in the live reveal show.”

So lore, rules, and more miniatures are all coming at the end of the week.

The Rumours Were Right

This one didn’t come out of nowhere. Drolf Ironhead, a hero from Warhammer Quest: Darkwater released earlier this year, had already hinted that a faction like this might be on the way. The leaked web images confirmed what fans had been speculating about for months.

Why Fans Are Excited

For longtime Warhammer players, this feels like a homecoming. The Old World’s classic dwarves have been missing from Age of Sigmar, and the Khazalite Holds look like a proper spiritual successor — much like how the Lumineth Realm-lords gave High Elf fans a new home in the Mortal Realms.

The full reveal is expected at Friday’s live show.

title: D&D Head Dan Ayoub Opens Up on the OGL: “Trust Takes a Long Time to Build and a Second to Break”
content:
Three years after the OGL crisis, Wizards of the Coast is still working to win back the tabletop community — and the man running D&D says he knows the clock is ticking.

Dan Ayoub, who took over as Head of Dungeons & Dragons in 2025, spoke with Wargamer’s Mollie Russell about the fallout from the OGL, the lessons learned since, and the new direction he’s steering the brand toward.

A Candid Admission

Ayoub didn’t dance around the subject when asked where Wizards went wrong with the OGL. He said the company lost sight of who D&D actually belongs to.

“It was a rug pull, right?” Ayoub told Wargamer. “A lot of people and businesses were built up around a specific thing. Trust was given to the brand, and people rightly felt the rug was pulled from under them.”

He also pointed to a broader mistake: assuming there’s a one-size-fits-all way to play D&D. Ayoub said his job isn’t to tell players how to run their games — it’s to give them the tools to do it their way.

Rebuilding Trust Won’t Be Quick

Ayoub describes his first year in charge as a mix of rewarding and terrifying, and he’s under no illusions about how long it takes to repair damaged trust.

“My biggest takeaway as I step into this role is that trust takes a long time to build and a second to break,” he said. “I’m keenly aware it’s going to take me a long time to repair this.”

If he deserves credit for one thing so far, he says it’s listening. Wizards established a community council, and Ayoub has personally spent time talking with fans, retailers, and consumers.

The Fallout Reshaped Everything

The OGL controversy didn’t stay contained to Wizards — it sent ripples through the entire industry, from Creative Commons releases to Pathfinder moving away from OGL-based rules. Ayoub compared it to a cataclysmic event from D&D’s own lore.

“I’m a big Dragonlance fan, and it was kind of like when the mountain dropped and reshaped the geography,” he said. “It fundamentally changed the ecosystem and everything about it.”

Stepping into the role afterward wasn’t easy. Ayoub called it “fucking terrifying,” admitting he was worried about damaging something he’s loved his whole life. But that love is exactly why he took the job — he wants to get D&D back to how he remembers it.

Bringing Outside Voices Back In

A major part of the new direction is collaboration. Wizards has been reaching out to classic creators like Margaret Weis, Tracy Hickman, Bob Salvatore, and Luke Gygax, along with partners like Ghostfire Gaming, which is taking on Ravenloft. Ayoub said he doesn’t want Wizards to be the only voice for D&D.

“The voice of D&D was only coming from one place, but that’s not how D&D grows,” he said. “I want to bring more people in to tell more stories.”

He noted the irony of it all, given D&D’s most famous advice: “The fundamental mantra is don’t split the party, and we went ahead and split the party.”

The Community Group Is Already Making a Difference

The D&D Community Advisory Group, launched in June, has been giving Wizards direct — and blunt — feedback. Ayoub said one early note changed how the company operates: members told him Wizards was doing cool things but doing a terrible job telling people about them. That led directly to publicizing the roadmap.

The group has even scrapped product ideas before they reached players. Ayoub values having people who’ll tell him when something isn’t working.

Looking Ahead

Ayoub says he’s never going to stop listening, and he’s holding himself to the promises he made when he took the role. He’s also thinking long-term — someone will eventually sit in his chair and celebrate D&D’s 100th anniversary, and that only happens if the game keeps growing.

The full interview, which also covers D&D’s franchise model, the Netflix and HBO projects, and how Ayoub is opening doors for new designers, is available at Wargamer.

title: Steve Jackson Steps Down as CEO After 46 Years
content:
Steve Jackson is handing over the reins. The founder of Steve Jackson Games is stepping down as CEO after leading the company for 46 years, returning to what he’s always loved most: designing games.

Sabrina Gonzalez, a longtime SJG staffer, is taking over as CEO. Allison Page, previously Managing Editor, has been promoted to Chief Operating Officer.

The news was announced Friday, September 11, 2026, via press release and a follow-up post on the company’s blog, the Daily Illuminator. SJG is inviting fans to drop by their forums and congratulate both Gonzalez and Page on their new roles.

The End of an Era

Jackson founded SJG in 1980 after several years at Metagaming, and his fingerprints are all over the tabletop hobby. He created GURPS (Generic Universal Role Playing System) in 1983 — a genre-agnostic RPG now in its fourth edition, which Jackson and line editor Sean Punch have continually refined over the decades.

Other staples from his design career include the party favourite Munchkin, the quick-playing Zombie Dice, and the sci-fi wargame Ogre.

Jackson ran the company with an unusual degree of transparency, publishing yearly “report to stakeholders” blog posts. But SJG has struggled to keep pace with the wider industry in recent years — a challenge reflected in both its public-facing identity and its ability to pull in new customers. Modern players tend to gravitate toward either experimental indie titles or established giants like D&D and Pathfinder.

Jackson was always a designer first and a business owner out of necessity. Handing the CEO role to Gonzalez may give the company room to get back to what it does best.

Who Is Sabrina Gonzalez?

Gonzalez joined SJG in 2013 and has been with the company ever since, aside from a brief 2025 detour into game manufacturing that broadened her view of that side of the business. She’s held roles including Production Artist and Production Manager, and has sat on the company’s Board of Directors since 2021.

As for her goals, she’s thinking about both the future and the past. “As a general goal, I’d like us to continue to grow,” she said. “We weathered the pandemic and pivoted project plans to address continually changing tariffs. The goal is always to make great games that people love. I want to continue developing new titles for future generations of gamers and also support (and sometimes update) the classics that our fans continue to request.”

That dual approach is already taking shape. SJG recently struck a deal with Possum Creek Games to publish and sell its RPG catalogue, including Wanderhome and Yazeba’s Bed & Breakfast, bringing on Jay Dragon as lead game designer and Ruby Lavin as art director. The company has also licensed indie RPGs like Luke Jordan’s Grand Guignol and Caro Acersion’s Last Train to Bremen.

Away from the desk, Gonzalez is a fan of party and dice games — dominoes is her all-time favourite and travels with her. She’s also a multi-instrumentalist who plays guitar, piano, ukulele, and more.

One of her fondest SJG memories: one of her first assignments was designing everything for the Munchkin Tavern, from the logo to the signage and menus. A photo of the 2013 Tavern logo ended up on a T-shirt signed by many attendees that year — a memento that reminds her of good times with people who are no longer with us. “We still think of and miss you greatly, Andrew Hackard,” she said.

Who Is Allison Page?

Page joined SJG in 2023 as Managing Editor. Before that, she was Executive Artistic Director of Killing My Lobster, a San Francisco sketch comedy outfit, and worked as a Narrative Designer in video games — her entry point into the industry.

Like Gonzalez, Page gravitates toward party games. She describes herself as fiercely competitive and happy to take any excuse to shout and laugh. She’s been a comedy writer and playwright for over a decade, spending much of her time writing, reading others’ work in her writing group, and hanging out with fellow writers complaining about writing — which she considers a crucial part of the craft.

What’s Next for SJG

A few things are already in motion:

  • Steve Jackson will focus on game design and development. No specific projects have been announced yet.
  • Dragon’s 7 Part Pact — a complex RPG about wizards governing an archipelago through baroque politics and a shaky balance of occult power — recently raised over $1,000,000 from nearly 5,800 backers. Fulfillment and retail are currently estimated for late 2027.
  • Munchkin 5.5E RPG, designed in partnership with Lynnvander Studios, is expected to hit Backerkit next month.

Both Gonzalez and Page say they’re ready for the challenge and looking forward to ushering in a new era for the company.

title: D&D Delves Back Into the Underdark With New Playtest Options
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released a second round of Underdark-themed playtest material for Dungeons & Dragons, and it’s packed with new ways to build a character from the deep places of the world.

The new Unearthed Arcana: Underdark Options 2 PDF introduces three subclasses and five new species, all drawing on the strange, dangerous corners of D&D’s most storied subterranean setting. The survey opens on D&D Beyond starting September 17, so there’s time to test these options at your table before weighing in.

Three New Subclasses

The playtest features a mix of brand-new concepts and one returning favourite:

  • Freedom Domain (Cleric) — A high-Dexterity Cleric built around liberation, movement, and breaking chains. Its spell list was designed with a single question in mind: would this spell help in a jailbreak? Channel Divinity lets allies shake off conditions like Frightened, Grappled, Paralyzed, or Restrained and reposition without provoking opportunity attacks.
  • Circle of Spores (Druid) — An update to the subclass originally from Guildmaster’s Guide to Ravnica and Tasha’s Cauldron of Everything, now tuned for 5.5e. The Underdark version leans harder into the myconid connection, granting Telepathy and reworking the old Spreading Spores feature into Explosive Burst — which makes your zombies detonate in a cloud of damaging spores when they die.
  • Faerzress Sorcery (Sorcerer) — Built around faerzress, the weird magical radiation of the Underdark. This Sorcerer can create zones of faerzress, ignore its drawbacks, and eventually transform into a being of pure faerzress energy. Lightning damage is the subclass’s signature flavour.

Five New Species

The species lineup is where things get really interesting. Rather than playing visitors from the surface, these options let you play characters who already call the Underdark home:

  • Deep Imaskari — Descendants of humans who fled into the depths millennia ago, now infused with the magic of “Unlight.” They create light rather than relying on Darkvision, and gain a versatile Aura of Unlight at level 3.
  • Drider — The classic drow-spider hybrid, finally playable. You get Spider Climb, Web Walker, and spells of the Spider Queen, with mechanics inspired by the Centaur from Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse.
  • Illithidkin — Victims (or willing participants) of mind flayer experimentation. They get psionic abilities, Psychic resistance, and telepathy. Notably, this is a separate route from the Ceremorphosis feat path in the previous UA, not meant to be combined with it.
  • Kuo-toa — Fishlike humanoids with a talent for creating bizarre, sometimes living idols. Their Deific Manifestation feature lets you cast Find Familiar and mix and match traits from two different forms to build your own little abomination.
  • Myconid — Bipedal fungal folk and the ultimate team players. Their abilities focus on building rapport, sharing knowledge, and granting the whole party telepathy through spores.

What the Design Team Is Saying

Senior Game Designer Jason Tondro noted that this UA touches on elements of the Underdark that have appeared before but are being “expanded or transformed in ways we’re not yet ready to fully reveal.” Faerzress, for example, dates back to 1978’s D1 Descent into the Depths of the Earth, while the Deep Imaskari first appeared in 2003’s Underdark supplement.

The material uses the Player’s Handbook rules, and Wizards is clear that these options are experimental — they may end up more or less powerful than what’s currently in the game, and could change significantly before any official publication.

How to Get Involved

If you want to help shape what makes it into a future D&D book, now’s your chance. Try these subclasses and species in your campaign or a one-shot, then fill out the survey on D&D Beyond when it goes live on September 17.

Worth noting: the document includes a content warning for body horror and mind control, so keep that in mind depending on your table.

title: Discworld Returns to the Tabletop with New Modiphius RPG
content:
Modiphius Entertainment is heading back to the Disc — and this time it’s trading the cobbled streets of Ankh-Morpork for the hills, forests, and castles of the Ramtops.

The publisher has announced Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald, a brand-new tabletop RPG launching on Gamefound this October. It follows the success of Discworld: Adventures in Ankh Morpork, which raised over £2m on Kickstarter during its 2025 campaign.

A Standalone Trip to the Ramtops

The good news for newcomers: you won’t need the first book to jump in. Adventures in Lancre and Überwald is a standalone core rulebook, playable with or without its predecessor. That makes it an easy entry point for anyone who’s been curious about Discworld roleplaying but didn’t back the original campaign.

The new book explores three iconic corners of Terry Pratchett’s world:

  • Lancre — home turf of the witches
  • Überwald — the gloomy, vampire-heavy region beyond the mountains
  • The Chalk — the rural downland region introduced in the later Discworld novels

Play as Witches, Vampires, Trolls, and Werewolves

Players will be able to encounter — and play as — witches, vampires, trolls, and werewolves, opening up a much wider range of character options than before. The book also brings in plenty of fan-favourite characters and locations, from the Ogg clan to Don’tgonearthe Castle to Granny Weatherwax herself.

For the first time in the official Discworld RPG line, there are also full rules for running ongoing campaigns, plus a book of linked adventures that takes players on a tour of the Ramtops.

What’s in the Campaign

Modiphius is promising a hefty spread of options when the Gamefound campaign goes live in October, including:

  • A hardcover core rulebook in standard and collector’s editions
  • An adventure book
  • A GM Toolkit
  • Additional supplements
  • Dice

The publisher is also putting extra focus on onboarding. The book includes expanded guidance and support for new players and gamemasters, with more examples that lean into the humour and wit Pratchett’s series is known for. There are also expanded rules for complex challenges, new risks for taking multiple consequences, and plenty of common situations explained in full — all of which Modiphius is billing as the easiest entry point yet for newcomers to both Discworld and tabletop RPGs in general.

More Discworld on the Way

This isn’t the only Discworld project in Modiphius’s pipeline. The publisher also has Kill Sam Vimes, a light board game about pursuing the titular character, and Readers Digested, a licensed edition of Reiner Knizia’s Blue Moon City, both available to pre-order now.

The Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald Gamefound campaign launches in October.

title: Wizards of the Coast Releases Exodus TTRPG, Tying Into Upcoming Sci-Fi Video Game
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released Exodus, a new sci-fi tabletop RPG set in the same universe as the upcoming AAA video game from Archetype Entertainment. The Traveler’s Handbook and Exodus Encyclopedia are now available for purchase through the official Exodus webpage.

Designed by James Ohlen—the veteran RPG designer behind Baldur’s Gate 2, Dragon Age: Origins, and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic—the game adapts the 5E system for sci-fi play, with new classes, weapons, and factions. The Traveler’s Handbook introduces eight origins, four classes with two subclasses each, and six powerful Traveler Dynasties that serve as in-game factions. The Exodus Encyclopedia packs in stat blocks for constructs, Celestials, changelings, awakened beings, and human NPCs, along with Remnant items for research and combat.

Both books are full-color hardcovers with Smythe sewn binding and spot UV finishing. The project also features contributions from award-winning sci-fi authors Adrian Tchaikovsky and Peter F. Hamilton.

The Exodus video game is slated for release in 2026 on PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S.

title: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana Returns – Chaosium’s Definitive Mythos Guide Hits in October
content:
Chaosium is releasing a new fourth edition of The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana this October, bringing the definitive guide to Lovecraftian horror back to shelves in full-color hardback format.

First published in 1994 and updated several times since, the book compiles detailed entries on mythos deities, creatures, tomes, and artifacts—from Azathoth to Zylac—tracing their appearances across fiction and pop culture. This new edition features updated text, evocative interior art, and a cover by John Sumrow, along with a fresh essay from author Dan Harms on the question “What is the Cthulhu Mythos?” Timelines of the Necronomicon, a cosmic horror bibliography, and illustrations of Nyarlathotep, Hastur, and Cthulhu himself round out the package.

The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana releases October 28—just in time to send a shiver down your spine before Halloween.

title: CMON Faces Make-or-Break Moment as It Warns of “Prolonged Structural Downturn”
content:
CMON has issued a stark warning about its future, telling investors its core business is stuck in a “prolonged structural downturn” and still burning through more cash than it brings in. The tabletop crowdfunding giant is now racing to raise up to $17.5m from outside investors.

The warning landed alongside CMON’s H1 financial report, and it caps off a brutal 18 months for one of the biggest names in crowdfunded board games.

Parts of this article is based on info from BoardGameWire.

A Company Half Its Former Size

CMON has spent the past year and a half trying to stop the bleeding. The publisher has:

  • Cut its workforce in half
  • Sold off major IP including Zombicide, Blood Rage, and Cthulhu: Death May Die
  • Shut down its Singapore office
  • Halted new crowdfunding campaigns

Those moves have helped — but not enough to fix the underlying problem.

Losses Shrinking, But Cash Still Draining

The good news: CMON’s losses are shrinking fast.

The company posted a loss of just over $2m in the first half of 2026, compared to nearly $7m during the same stretch last year. Revenue also crept up more than 7% year-on-year, hitting $3.68m. Selling and distribution costs were cut by more than half, and administrative expenses dropped from $4.37m to $2.37m.

The bad news: it’s still not enough to keep the lights on without outside help.

CMON’s cash reserves have been in freefall. They sat at $3.9m at the end of 2022, fell to $2.1m by the end of 2024, and slipped to just over $900,000 by June 2025. In early August, the company revealed it had roughly $368,000 on hand — less than a month’s worth of operating expenses.

The Backer Problem: $14m in Undelivered Games

A huge chunk of CMON’s financial pressure comes down to games that backers have already paid for but haven’t received.

Eight crowdfunded titles remain undelivered, representing $14m raised from backers. The two biggest are **DC Super Heroes United** (over $4.4m raised) and DCeased (over $2.5m). Both were originally due last year, but have been delayed repeatedly and are now slated for Q1 2027.

CMON hasn’t completed fulfillment on a crowdfunding project since Zombicide: White Death in mid-2025. It has managed to ship some pre-orders — Cthulhu: Dark Providence, Marvel United: Witching Hour, and Dune: Desert War all went out in the first half of this year — but four more pre-order titles remain in limbo, including the Assassin’s Creed Role Playing Game.

The $17.5m Gamble

To stay afloat, CMON is leaning on a massive rights issue designed to raise up to HK$150.5m (about $19m). The plan lets existing shareholders buy three new shares for every one they already own.

There’s just one problem: shareholders barely took the bait. Only 7.76% of the new shares were claimed by the August deadline, leaving CMON scrambling to find more than $17.5m from other investors — a figure approaching 2.5-times the company’s entire valuation from its last share sale in February.

If the money comes through, here’s how CMON plans to spend it:

  • 40% — Day-to-day operations for roughly a year, including staff, royalties, shipping, and distribution
  • 20% — Paying down debts, including $2.46m owed to a company director and $385,000 in unsecured employee advances
  • 25% — Expansion into existing and new markets, with a focus on Europe, Japan, and the Philippines
  • 15% — Potential acquisitions in digital gaming

The final result of the rights issue is due September 15.

A Digital Pivot — With a Catch

That 15% digital acquisition budget is notable, especially since CMON just walked away from a planned $2.1m investment in NFT game maker Blissful Link. That deal would have valued Blissful Link at over $95m — despite the company posting a loss of about $197,000 in 2024 on revenues of just over $408,000.

CMON says it’s now hunting for one to three businesses, mostly in Asia-Pacific, valued between $1.3m and $2.5m each, to help build digital adaptations and companion apps. The publisher insists physical tabletop games remain its core business and that digital is meant to complement, not replace, them.

Where the Money Comes From Now

The report also lays bare just how dramatically CMON’s geographic revenue has shifted.

North America generated over $8.6m in the first half of 2021 — 57% of the company’s roughly $15.1m revenue at the time. By the first half of 2026, North and South America combined brought in just $642,000.

Europe has collapsed similarly, falling from about $4.5m to $982,000 over the same period.

Asia is now CMON’s largest market by a wide margin, generating over $2m and accounting for about 55% of total revenue — up from less than 10% in 2021. That’s not because Asia is growing, though. Revenue there is down roughly 37% since 2022. It’s just fallen far less than everywhere else.

What’s Next for Crowdfunding?

CMON said back in March that it intended to resume crowdfunding in the second half of 2026. Its latest report doesn’t repeat that promise. Instead, the company says new titles will be developed and launched “selectively” based on market conditions, available cash, and project readiness.

For a publisher built on the crowdfunding model, that’s a notable shift in tone — and a sign that CMON’s road back to stability is still a long one.

title: This Monty Python-esque comedy RPG lets you improv as a band of incompetent and dangerously powerful wizards
content:
Hello Wizard I Have a Problem is a new tabletop roleplaying game that allows players to become powerful and incompetent spellcasters.

The upcoming roleplaying game sees any number of players collaborating together to tell a story about a band of chaotic wizards. Similarly to the likes of absurdist, fantastical comedy such as the works of iconic British group Monty Python, alongside the likes of The Mighty Boosh and What We Do in the Shadows, Hello Wizard I have a Problem is all about rapid scenes infused by the strange and unexpected.

Unlike many other tabletop RPGs, Hello Wizard sees its players taking turns to take on the roles of player character and games master. Each scene in Hello Wizard has a single player take the spotlight as their spellcaster, with the goal of impressing their fellow sorcerers with their magic. The active player describes what spells their wizard casts, with the other players acting collectively as a GM and deciding how these spells can go wrong.

Players will use a Problem Generator included in the fantasy RPG’s rulebook as inspiration for what could go wrong with the wizards’ spells, with the book capable of making over “200,000” prompts for possible disastrous outcomes. Once every player has had the opportunity to step into the spellcasting spotlight at least a few times, the game ends and players tally up their ‘points’ - which are decided by a loose improv system - and determine who is the most impressive wizard.

The rules system for Hello Wizard is very straightforward and intended to be easy for players to learn. Setup for the tabletop RPG is also designed to be quick and easy, with players expected to start in little time. The rulebook for the game will contain advice and optional rules players can use to augment their playthroughs too.

Hello Wizard I have a Problem was created by Sam Armstrong, a tabletop RPG designer who has previously made titles such as All Bastard - a fantasy TRPG in which players take the roles of either a band of bragging heroes or the bastards they defeated - and horror roleplaying game Slasher. The artwork for the game was created by illustrator Evlyn Moreau, who has previously worked on RPGs like Liminal High School.

The crowdfunding campaign for Hello Wizard I Have a Problem is on Kickstarter until later this afternoon, with the title potentially being made available on Armstrong’s Itch.io page. A pledge of £8 ($10) will get backers a physical copy of the game in June, alternatively a PDF version is available for £4 ($5).

title: Re-enact Greta Gerwig’s Little Women with this coming-of-age tabletop RPG
content:
New tabletop roleplaying game, Castles in the Air, will enable players to re-enact their favourite coming-of-age stories.

Castles in the Air was inspired by the likes of classic coming-of-age period dramas such as Little Women by Louisa May Alcott - which was adapted into a 2019 film directed by Greta Gerwig and starring Saoirse Ronan, Emma Watson, Florence Pugh, Laura Dern and Timothee Chalamet - and Anne of Green Gables by Lucy Maud Montgomery, which was adapted into a televisions series in 2017 by Netflix.

The upcoming roleplaying game will see players’ characters grow up together from children to adults during the historical era known as the Gilded Age, which took place in the USA from the 1870s to the 1890s and saw an increase in industrialisation, economic growth and migration to the US. Castles in the Air is a collaborative storytelling game in which players construct narratives that centre around the wonders and fears of childhood, before tackling the joys and hardships of adulthood.

Players begin the tabletop RPG as a tight-knit group of children, all of whom have great expectations of their futures and much quieter current lives. In this phase of the story, players develop a shared childhood together by doing the things rural and financially supported kids did during that era: like playing in their local farmlands, swimming in the lakes and watching the stars.

As the player characters grow up, they’ll begin exploring other feelings and ideas that come with age. Characters in the group might develop a crush on someone or form a heated rivalry with one of the other local children. All the while, the player group will grow up together, before eventually reaching adulthood and potentially finding themselves drifting apart as life takes them in different directions - perhaps to only meet once again.

Players will be able to create their characters in Castles in the Air by choosing from a variety of character roles inspired by classic archetypes, such as the troublesome scamp, studious bookworm or spoiled princess. Add onto this a dream, childhood relationships, a family background and a bosom enemy, and players can even create their favourite characters from the likes of Little Women or Anne of Green Gables.

Castles in the Air was designed and written by Melia Carraway, with contributions from co-created by the co-founders of the RPG’s publisher, Storybrewer’s Roleplaying, Vee Hendro and Hayley Gordon, who also co-designed Good Society: a tabletop RPG inspired by the works of Jane Austen.

The crowdfunding campaign for Castles in the Air is on Kickstarter until June 9th, with a pledge of AU$ 99 (£52/$77) getting backers a physical copy of the game in March 2025. Alternatively, players can get a digital version for a pledge of AU$ 34 (£18/$26).
